bio.en: Jessica Livingston is the co-founder of Y Combinator—the first and most famous startup accelerator, which has funded 5,000+ companies including Airbnb, Stripe, and Coinbase—and author of Founders at Work; she is famed for her 'social radar' for reading people.
bio.zh: Jessica Livingston 是 Y Combinator 的联合创始人——这是第一家也是最著名的创业加速器，已投资 5000 多家公司，包括 Airbnb、Stripe、Coinbase——也是《Founders at Work》的作者；她以善于“读人”的“社交雷达”而闻名。

summary.en: Jessica reveals the superpower behind her 'Social Radar' nickname: an uncanny ability to read founders (do the co-founders get along? do they get defensive? are they hustlers who'll burn the boat?). She shares wild early YC stories—including how the Airbnb founders won the partners over with their Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's cereal boxes—and how being defensively committed signals trouble. The episode also covers her Social Radars podcast and a fun 'reading the mind in the eyes' test, with tips on developing your own people-reading ability.
summary.zh: Jessica 揭开了她“社交雷达”绰号背后的超能力：一种读创始人的惊人本领（联合创始人处得来吗？他们会防御性地辩解吗？他们是会破釜沉舟的实干家吗？）。她分享了 YC 早期的疯狂故事——包括 Airbnb 创始人如何用“Obama O's”和“Cap'n McCain's”麦片盒征服合伙人，以及“防御性过强”如何预示麻烦。这期节目还涵盖了她的 Social Radars 播客和一个有趣的“读眼识心”测试，并给出培养读人能力的建议。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: My three co-founders were deeply technical, but I would look at other things about founders. All these little social cues.
turns.zh: 我的三位联合创始人都是技术大牛，但我会关注创始人身上其他的特质。那些细微的社交暗示至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your nickname was the Social Radar. Every interview, everyone always turned to you and they're like, "Jessica, what does their social radar say?"

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I would look at, do the co-founders get along? Are these people committed? And if a founder would get defensive, that was always a bad sign.
turns.zh: 我会观察联合创始人是否合拍，他们是否全身心投入。如果创始人开始自我防卫，这往往是个不好的信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else along the Airbnb story that would be interesting to share?
turns.zh: 关于Airbnb的故事，还有哪些有趣的细节可以分享？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: He hated their idea, and Paul tried to get Brian and Joe and Nate to change it. But I remember specifically Joe brought out the cereal boxes, the Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's, and I just thought, oh my God, they're going to work hard to do whatever they can to make this company succeed.
turns.zh: 他讨厌他们的创意，保罗试图说服布莱恩、乔和内特改方案。但我清楚记得乔拿出麦片盒子——奥巴马麦片和麦凯恩船长麦片——那一刻，我心想，天哪，他们肯定会全力以赴让公司成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You just talk a bit about this idea of just making shit happen, showing signs of being hustlers.
turns.zh: 你可以谈谈"让事情成真"的理念，展现出创业者的拼劲。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Do you sort of need that desperation. You have to burn the boat.
turns.zh: 你必须有那种紧迫感。你必须破釜沉舟。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I will try Lenny, I will try. I don't talk much about it because it's hard to talk about. I don't understand. It's hard to put into words exactly what it is about me, but it's true that my nickname at Y Combinator was the Social Radar. And I think it was because my three co-founders were deeply technical people, and I was not. But I would look at other things about founders. When we'd have these 10-minute interviews, I would look at, do the co-founders get along? Are these people committed? Do they really know about their product? Do they care? Are they going to quit their job? Or are they telling us that they are going to quit their job, but really aren't? All these little social cues that I'd try to pick up on. (00:09:10): And in a lot of cases, red flags about them that I'd add to the decision-making process. And so that's why they called me the Social Radar, and it just sort of stuck. And it's because I love people and the dynamics and understanding what's motivating people. I just love it and I love founder psychology, founders personalities. I am absolutely fascinated with it.
turns.zh: 我会试试看的，我会努力的。我不常谈论这件事，因为它很难启齿。我不明白。很难用语言准确描述我身上到底有什么特质，但确实我在Y Combinator的昵称是“社交雷达”。我想这是因为我的三位联合创始人都是技术型人才，而我不是。但我会观察创始人的其他方面。在我们进行10分钟面试时，我会留意：联合创始人相处融洽吗？他们是否全心投入？他们对产品真心了解吗？他们是否用心经营？他们会辞去现职吗？还是说他们只是口头说要辞职，实际上却另有打算？这些细微的社交信号，我都会努力捕捉。（00:09:10）在很多情况下，我会把这些预警信号纳入决策过程。这就是为什么他们叫我“社交雷达”，这个称号就这么流行开来了。因为我热爱与人打交道，喜欢观察人际动态，理解人们的动机。我对此乐在其中，还热衷于研究创始人的心理和性格。我对此简直着迷。

What does their social radar say?" Can you just talk a bit about that role that you played in the early days of YC of kind of seeing that side of candidates?
turns.zh: 你曾在某处写道——保罗也提到过，还有其他人也说过——在YC早期做的每场面试，大家都会把目光投向你，问：“杰西卡，你怎么看？你的‘社交雷达’怎么说？”能否谈谈你在YC早期扮演的这个角色，如何洞察候选人的这方面特质？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Well, in the early days, especially before I knew a lot, as much as I know now, about startups and founders, early on, I was learning a lot in the first few years. And in the first few years, it was just the four of us. So I would be in charge of going out telling people, "Wait here while we do the interview, come on in." I'd be in charge of the stopwatch that would time us. And I'd say, "Okay, our time's up." And it was very administrative, and I would observe. Paul, Robert and Trevor, my co-founders would be asking them all sorts of questions about their product and their technology and blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. I would occasionally ask questions, but I'd usually remain pretty silent. And so I don't think people even really noticed me. But I would be just watching them and sort of trying to observe as much as I could, not understanding sometimes even the technology that they were talking about. I let my co-founders do that. (00:11:06): And then after, we'd be talking, they'd look at me and they'd be like, "Should we fund them? Jessica, should we fund them?" And sometimes I could tell based on the conversation whether they thought that the technology was good or how they felt, and sometimes I'd say, "Absolutely we should." Or sometimes I'd say, "Guys, I'm a little nervous. Did you see how that founder interrupted the other founder and wouldn't let the other founder talk?" Because my three co-founders sometimes wouldn't notice this. (00:11:39): They'd be so caught up in the conversation they were having about the technology, especially Paul. Paul would get really into things. And sometimes I always tease Paul, because one of his defining qualities is that sometimes someone would have an idea that he'd get so excited about that by the end of the interview he'd be giving them ideas about how to grow their product and what they could become. And they'd sit there saying, "Yeah, yeah, that's a great idea." And then he'd say, "Fund them." And I'd say, "Whoa, whoa, whoa, Paul, you can't just fund this because you love the idea. Let's take a step back and let's look. Like these two founders are working at Google and they don't say they're going to quit. That's not good." And I'd point out these things that I had observed. But I mean, we always agreed. It was very rare that we wouldn't agree on funding something. We were usually on the same page.
turns.zh: 嗯，在早期阶段，尤其是当我对创业公司和创始人还没有像现在这样深入了解之前，头几年我学到了很多东西。最初只有我们四个人团队。我会负责外出接待客户，说：“请在此处等候，我们要进行采访了，请进来。”我还要负责计时器，监督面试时长。然后我会说：“好的，时间到了。” 这整个过程非常行政化，而我主要负责观察。我的联合创始人保罗、罗伯特和特雷弗会询问客户关于产品和技术的各种问题。我偶尔也会提问，但大部分时间都保持沉默。我觉得人们甚至没怎么注意到我。不过我会仔细观察他们，有时甚至连他们谈论的技术我都听不太懂，我就让联合创始人去处理这些问题。（00:11:06）  之后，我们会讨论，他们会看着我说：“我们应该投资他们吗？杰西卡，我们该不该投资他们？”有时我能从对话中判断出他们对技术的看法，有时我会说：“绝对应该投资。”有时我会说：“伙计们，我有点紧张。你看到那个创始人打断另一个创始人，不让对方说话了吗？” 因为我的三个联合创始人有时会忽略这些细节。他们太专注于技术讨论了，尤其是保罗。保罗总是很投入。有时我会取笑他，因为他的一个特点是，有时有人提出的一个想法会让他兴奋不已，以至于到采访结束时，他会给对方提供如何发展产品和未来发展的建议。而对方只会说一句：“是啊，是啊，这个主意不错。” 然后保罗会说：“投资他们吧。” 我会说：“等等，等等，保罗，你不能因为喜欢这个想法就随便投资。我们得退一步看看。比如这两个创始人在谷歌工作，他们又没说要辞职。这可不行啊。” 我会指出我观察到的问题。不过我们总能达成一致。很少会对投资事宜产生分歧。我们通常意见一致。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. It's interesting that you talk about these behaviors, co-founders interrupting each other, or being kind of aggressive here and there. Some people believe that's okay for founders to be like this. A lot of successful founders, Elon, for example, Steve Jobs, who are kind of assholes a lot of times, I imagine, and I've read part of the reason you thought about just the type of person is you're trying to build a specific culture in the early days of YC and you're going to be around these people. So maybe can you talk a bit about just why those elements were important to you and why'd you look for those?
turns.zh: 我明白了。你谈到这些行为，比如联合创始人互相打断，或者时不时有点强势。有些人认为创业者这样做没关系。很多成功的创始人，比如埃隆、史蒂夫·乔布斯，据我所知，他们很多时候都挺难相处的。我读到过，你之所以要特定类型的创始人，部分原因是YC早期要建立一种特定的文化，而你会和这些人共处。所以能否请你谈谈这些要素为何对你如此重要，以及你为何要寻找这些特质？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I've definitely heard that Steve Jobs could be an. I've heard stories. But I think I would've funded him because he's so incredible and he was so smart and so interested in the product and knew... I'm very persuaded by people who know what they're talking about and love their product and are domain experts. But I did consciously, especially early on, less so later on, early on, I did sometimes tend to say, "I really think this person's an asshole, I do not want to fund them." And we often wouldn't. And very early on when we were just funding 10, 20, 30 startups a batch, sometimes I have been known to say, "I don't know if I can have dinner with them every week." It was that point. And I don't think we've ever regretted any of those. It didn't happen all the time, that was rare. But life's too short, and I wanted to be able to work with these founders. (00:14:16): And as it turns out, it was sort of important early on in weeding out explicit assholes because that was the basis of our Y Combinator community, which is now thousands of founders. Now, of course, all the founders aren't all running their company anymore, but I would say most all of the founders bring something useful and valuable to the table. So if you ask a question on Bookface, on our forum for founders, someone is going to be there to help you. And it's amazing. And that all started very early on, there was this culture of older batch mates helping newer ones, and this pay-it-forward mentality where everyone helped one another and rooted for one another and made introductions for each other. And I think it's a big part of our Y Combinator community now.
turns.zh: 我确实听说过史蒂夫·乔布斯可能是个混蛋。我听过一些故事。但我认为我会投资他，因为他太了不起了，他非常聪明，对产品充满热情，而且……我对那些对自己所谈论的内容了如指掌、热爱自己的产品且是领域专家的创业者深信不疑。不过我确实有意识地这么做过，尤其是在早期阶段，后来就没那么频繁了。早期阶段，我有时会说：“我真的觉得这个人是个混蛋，我不想投资他们。”我们通常也不会投资他们。早期阶段，我们每批资助10、20、30家初创公司时，我曾坦言：“我不知道能否每周和他们共进晚餐。”当时就是这种情况。我觉得我们从未后悔过任何一次这样的决定。虽然这种情况并不常见，但人生短暂，我希望能与这些创始人合作。（00:14:16）事实证明，早期阶段就能识别出那些明显的混蛋非常重要，因为这是我们Y Combinator社区的基础，如今这个社区已汇聚了数千名创始人。当然，现在并非所有创始人都还在经营自己的公司，但我可以说，绝大多数创始人都能为项目带来有用且有价值的贡献。比如，如果你在Bookface（我们的创始人论坛）上提问，总会有人愿意帮助你。这真是令人惊叹。而这一切始于早期阶段，那时就有一种老批次成员帮助新批次成员的文化，以及一种互帮互助、相互支持、为彼此牵线搭桥的奉献精神。我认为这正是我们Y Combinator社区如今的重要组成部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I wrote down a few of the things that you mentioned you look for, and you looked for in the early days. So let me just share a few of them and let's spend a little more time here. So you looked for, did the founders get along? Are they committed to the idea? Are they ready to quit their job? Are there any red flags? So is there anything else that you remember you spent a lot of time thinking about or looking for then or even now?
turns.zh: 所以我记下了你提到的几项你在早期阶段寻找的要素。让我来分享其中几项，咱们再多花点时间讨论。那么你会关注哪些方面呢？比如创始人是否合得来？他们是否对项目充满热情？他们是否准备好辞去现有工作？有没有任何危险信号？还有其他什么你记得当时或现在花了很多时间思考或寻找的要素吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: There's looking for in the application and then there's looking for in the interview, and now we have software that looks for all of the red flags in the application that I used to do by hand. In the application, I'd look for just weird things, like was there a huge gap in the equity allocation? Did one founder have 99% and one founder have 1%? That's weird. I'd want to dig in on that. That doesn't feel right. Are they going to quit their job? Are they going to move to Silicon Valley? What are their current shareholders? Is like 90% of their company already owned by someone else? There all these weird things that we like to just flag. And we wouldn't necessarily not fund someone because of them, but it's just more data. So that was in the application that I'd look through all of those. (00:16:33): But in the interview I definitely was sort of, one thing I remember I would always look for was, when you'd have a conversation with us, a lot of times, Paul especially, but Robert and Trevor, would really be getting right into the idea and questioning you, and how do you know this? And what about this? And if a founder would get defensive, that was always a bad sign, always a bad sign. The best founders would say, "Gosh, I have thought about it and here's what I figured out." Or, they just have this almost a tennis match and a conversation rather than closing up and feeling like, oh, this person's interrogating me. You could just sort of, the open-mindedness, the flexible-mindedness of people was really important. I'd get really excited about domain expertise. Like my co-founders, we all loved that. If someone was fixing their own problem in a broken industry, we loved that. (00:17:39): Definitely, I'd look for co-founder relationships. And again, I'm not saying I was always right, but you could tell if... One founder, I'll give a story, one founder, once we asked a question and one person started to respond and the other founder put his arm in front of him and said, "I'll answer that question." And it was just so weird that he wouldn't let his co-founder speak. We'd have situations where we'd call people like hackers in a cage, where it's kind of obvious there'd be a business founder, business person, who had clearly convinced a programmer to join the team. They were given, the programmer was given, very little equity and just we called them programmers in a cage, like hackers in a cage. And sometimes that works out, I'm not saying it doesn't. But I'd always try to observe, okay, does this hacker in a cage have any say in the company, the direction of the product? That sort of thing. Because the programmer needs to have opinions.
turns.zh:
申请材料里要找问题，而面试中也要找问题。现在我们有软件能自动筛查申请材料中的所有危险信号——这些工作过去都是我手动完成的。在审核申请材料时，我会留意一些异常情况，比如股权分配是否存在巨大缺口？创始人之一持有99%股份，另一位只有1%，这就很可疑。我会深入调查这种不合理现象。还有，他们会辞去现职吗？会搬去硅谷吗？现有股东情况如何？公司90%的股份是否已被他人控股？这些奇怪的现象我们都需要标注出来。当然，我们不会因此拒绝投资，但这些信息能提供更多参考。所以在审核申请材料时，我会仔细检查所有这些细节。

（00:16:33）但在面试环节，我特别关注的一点是，当与候选人交流时，尤其是保罗、罗伯特和特雷弗，他们会深入探讨创意构想，提出诸多疑问。比如“你怎么知道这些信息？”“那又怎样？”如果创始人开始回避问题，这往往是个危险信号。优秀的创始人会坦诚回应：“嗯，我确实考虑过这个问题，这是我的结论。” 或者他们会展开一场类似网球比赛般的思维对话，避免封闭式提问，让人感觉不像是在质询对方。开放的思维和灵活的态度至关重要。我对行业专长充满热情，比如我的联合创始人团队就热爱这种模式——当有人在破碎的行业中解决自身痛点时，我们深受触动。

（00:17:39）我尤其关注创始人之间的合作关系。当然，我不能说自己每次判断都正确，但有些细节很能说明问题。比如，有位创始人在回答问题时，另一位创始人突然伸手挡住他说：“我来回答这个问题。”这种不让搭档发声的行为令人警觉。还有些案例类似“笼中黑客”，比如某位程序员加入团队却只获得极少股权，这类情况有时能成功，但我总会仔细观察：这位“笼中黑客”在公司战略方向上有发言权吗？因为程序员必须有自己的见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny. I love this metaphor. And I totally get what you mean. I want to unpack a couple of these, because this is exactly where I was hoping we'd go. So this idea of looking for defensiveness and being open to change and being flexible, why do you think that was so important to successful founders? Why did you look for that? Why was that a predictor of success?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。我特别喜欢这个比喻。我完全理解你的意思。我想深入探讨几个方面，因为这正是我们要讨论的核心。那么，寻找防御心理、开放变革、灵活应变的能力，为什么对成功的创始人如此重要？你为什么要关注这些？为什么这能预示成功？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Several things. First of all, being defensive is really bad, if you're a startup founder, because you're always going to get people who question you. And it's your job to educate them, if it's a new area, you're doing something presumably pretty new, you're always going to have people who question it or say, "That product's already out there, why is yours better?" You have to educate them. You don't want to be defensive about it. Also, a lot of times, the first idea isn't bang right on, the right idea, and you have to be open-minded and maybe adjust it in a certain direction. The famous PayPal story, how it started off being the PalmPilot, or money transfer. And money transfer between the PalmPilots or whatever. And then all the customers were using a janky version on the web, and they were begging for this to be on the web. And finally, the founder said, "Oh, I see what most people want this for." You have to be open-minded to see what direction really is what your users want. And so if you find someone is defensive, usually they're not open-minded. (00:20:26): The other thing is that the best founders will want to learn from other people and listen to other people. You talk to the Collison brothers and say something, they ask you a question, they're listening to your answer. So many founders think, oh, I can't learn from anyone. But the best founders are always listening and having spirited debates about things. I mean, that's part of the process. And so I think when someone's defensive, it's just a bad sign. So I would look for that. (00:21:01): I loved when I'd find someone sort of showcase that they'd make something happen no matter what; they're scrappy, they're hustlers. I remember... Can I tell the story about the Airbnb interview?
turns.zh:
好的，用户让我把一段英文翻译成中文。首先，我需要仔细阅读原文，理解每个句子的意思。这段文字主要讲初创公司创始人不要过于防守，要善于教育用户，适应市场变化，以及倾听他人的建议。

第一句提到防守心理对创业者不利，因为总会有人质疑你。这里“defensive”翻译成“防守”可能不太准确，可能需要用“固执”或者“不愿意接受批评”。接下来，“educate them”要翻译成“教育他们”，保持口语化。提到新领域时，“new area”可以译为“新领域”或“新兴领域”，根据上下文选择合适词汇。

第二段讲初始想法不一定正确，要保持开放心态调整方向。这里“janky version”可以译为“简陋版本”或“不成熟的版本”，根据语境选择合适词汇。PayPal的例子需要准确翻译产品名称和功能，比如“PalmPilot”应保留原名，可能需要加注释。

最后一段提到好的创始人愿意学习和倾听，他人质疑时要保持开放。这里“open-minded”翻译成“开放心态”比较合适。还要注意口语化的表达，比如“janky version”可能需要意译为“不成熟的版本”或“简陋版本”，根据上下文选择最合适的词汇。

整体需要保持专业术语的一致性，同时让翻译流畅自然。注意段落之间的衔接，确保逻辑清晰。最后检查有没有遗漏的部分，比如提到的Airbnb面试故事，需要确保翻译准确，保持故事的连贯性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Okay, because that was definitely one I'll never forget. That was one that was clear the founders were really good. The market had just crashed basically with all the banks going out of business and everything. And so we were only funding startups that we felt had really scrappy founders and could be cockroaches, meaning could live off of very little amounts of money, or could charge customers and make money. And we didn't fund that many people in that winter '09 batch. So we're being very strict with ourselves, very disciplined about things. And the Airbnb guys came in, and I just remember they had a contagious amount of energy. They just had an energy about them the way that they talked about their product, which was crazy at the time, staying in someone's bed or airbed. In fact, it's a famous part of the story, we hated their idea and Paul tried to get Brian and Joe and Nate to change it. So we didn't even like the idea. But I remember specifically they brought, at the end, Joe brought out these, the cereal boxes, the Obama O's and Cap'n Crunch's or Cap'n McCain's or whatever.
turns.zh: 好吧，那次经历绝对让我永生难忘。很明显，那些创始人确实非常出色。当时市场刚刚崩盘，所有银行都濒临倒闭。于是我们只资助那些拥有顽强拼搏精神的初创公司——他们就像蟑螂一样，能以极少的资金维持运营，或者向用户收费赚钱。2009年冬季那批融资项目，我们资助的人数不多。因此，我们对自己要求极其严格，执行力极强。Airbnb的团队一进来，我就记得他们充满感染力的活力。在谈论他们的产品时，他们那种热情真是令人惊叹——当时提出的住在别人床上或充气床垫上的概念简直疯狂。事实上，这段故事很有名，我们当时非常不看好他们的创意，保罗甚至试图说服布莱恩、乔和内特去改方案。但我特别记得，最后乔拿出了那些麦片盒子，还有奥巴马O型麦片和"船长麦克莱恩"之类的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cap'n McCain's, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，就是"船长麦克莱恩"。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Yeah, Cap'n McCain's. They were saying that they went to some Costco or something and bought off-brand Cheerios and off-brand Cap'n Crunch's, took them out of the box, put them in this new box, glue-gunned it shut. And I just thought, oh my God, these guys are really going to great lengths for this. And for some reason, it was silly, but it really appealed to me. They're going to work hard to do whatever they can to make this company succeed. And even though we were skeptical about the idea, I think we definitely made the right bet on the founders, and it was just very clear in that interview.
turns.zh: 是啊，麦凯恩船长的。他们说他们去了一家好市多之类的地方，买了非品牌的麦片，比如非品牌的Cheerios和Cap'n Crunch，把它们从原包装里拿出来，放进新盒子里，然后用胶枪封住。我当时就想，天哪，这些人真是下了血本啊。但不知为何，这事儿挺搞笑的，却让我特别感动。他们会竭尽全力让公司成功。尽管我们当时对这个想法心存疑虑，但我觉得我们当初对创始人的选择是对的，从那次采访就能看得清清楚楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm so happy you shared that story, I was definitely going to ask about it. It's so funny because I've heard that story at least a hundred times working at Airbnb, they tell the beginning of Airbnb every chance they get at every all-hands. It's like a recurring theme. And it's great to hear that basically it went exactly the way they describe. Oftentimes, there's a myth around what happened, but that's exactly how they describe it.
turns.zh: 真高兴你分享了这个故事，我正想问你呢。太有意思了，因为我在Airbnb工作时听过这个故事不下百遍，每次全员大会他们都会讲Airbnb的开创故事。这简直成了一个循环往复的主题。很高兴听到事情进展跟他们描述的完全一致。通常大家对具体细节会有误解，但他们讲的就是原原本本的故事。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: No, it was definitely a whole crazy story and how Paul called them to accept them, and they were on the 280 or something or the 101 and the reception went down. And so he didn't hear if they were accepted or not. Did he tell that part?
turns.zh: 对，整个故事真是太疯狂了。保罗打电话通知他们项目被接受时，他们正在280号公路或101号公路上开车，信号断断续续。结果他们没听到是否被接受的消息。他提到这部分了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I haven't heard that part.
turns.zh: 没有，我没听过这部分。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Oh yeah, that's part of the story. And they had to keep driving to get to talk to Paul again and find out that they were accepted. Oh, yeah. It was just a crazy interview.
turns.zh: 哦对，这也是故事的一部分。他们不得不继续开车，再次找到保罗确认项目被接受了。对，就是个疯狂的面试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The element of the story I'm also curious about is, the way Joe tells it, is he had the box in his backpack. And as they were walking out, Paul or you is like, "Hey, what's that? What's that cereal box doing there?" Is that how it went, or is it more like, "Hey, we have this cereal thing."?
turns.zh: 故事里有个细节我也很好奇。乔讲的时候说，他把盒子放在背包里。他们走出会议室时，保罗或者你会问：“嘿，那是什么？那个麦片盒子怎么在那儿？”是这样吗？还是他们直接说：“嘿，我们给你带了点小礼物。”？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I don't think Paul and I looked in his backpack and asked. I think there was definitely some pressure on Joe not to show us the cereal boxes. I think Nate was really down on that, especially. And I think they were walking out the door and they're like, "Hey, we just brought you a little something." I think Joe did pull it out, and we had an extra minute or so around the cereal boxes. That's how I heard about the glue gun story and everything. But I think Joe had been reluctant, but he did it at the end and I think it was a good call.
turns.zh: 我觉得保罗和我没翻他背包看。我记得Nate特别反对乔展示麦片盒子。他们走出会议室时说：“嘿，我们给你们带了点小礼物。”乔最后还是把盒子拿出来了，我们还围着麦片盒子多待了一分钟左右。我就是从那时听说了用胶枪的故事。但我觉得乔之前不太情愿，最后还是妥协了，这决定很明智。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so funny. And after that meeting, what was that conversation like between you and Paul? Was it just like everyone's like, "We definitely got to do this."? Or was it like you being like, "Hey, these guys are really interesting."?
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。那次会议之后，你和保罗的对话是怎样的？大家是不是都说：“我们一定要做成这件事。”？还是你觉得：“嘿，这些人真有趣。”？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: No, I think we all liked them. We all liked them. But I remember saying, "We have got to..." I just remember being like, "We've got to fund these guys. I don't know about the idea. Maybe they'll change their idea, who knows? But they seem really great." Again, the energy level and the passion with which they spoke about their experience hosting, because they'd been around struggling, but had been a company with an idea for a little while before they applied to YC. We were there basically their Hail Mary, their last resort for them. And so they could tell us about their story about how they hosted the people at a conference, and there was definitely some magic to it, which was convincing.
turns.zh: 没有，我觉得我们都喜欢他们。我们都喜欢他们。但我记得当时我说道，"我们必须得..." 我只记得当时自己在想，"我们得给这些人融资。我不确定他们的想法是否可行，也许他们会调整思路，谁知道呢？但他们看起来真的很棒。" 再说他们的活力和激情，他们谈论主办活动的经历时洋溢着热情，因为他们曾深陷困境，但在申请YC之前，他们的公司已经有了初步构想。我们当时基本上就是他们的最后一搏，是他们求生的稻草。所以他们能给我们讲述他们在会议上接待客人的故事，那种魔力确实令人信服。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else along the Airbnb story that would be interesting to share while we're on that topic?
turns.zh: 在Airbnb的故事之外，还有其他什么有趣的案例可以分享吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I mean, the only interesting thing as it relates to being the social radar is that there were just some interviews that I remember because I just thought, this is great. These founders are so good. I'm totally convinced. What they're working on might not work, but I feel like it's so worth the bet based on these founders. And that happened. There were definitely a couple other of our most successful companies that I clearly felt that way about. You just feel like they know what they're talking about, they thought about the problem. They're not solving this problem because it's sort of the problem du jour or fun and exciting. Some are very unsexy problems like when Parker Conrad applied with Zenefits, unsexy HR stuff, benefits stuff. But he knew how broken it was and was trying to fix it. And I love stories like that. There was one story in terms of... The one time I did sort of persuade the rest of the group to fund someone was, do you know the company GOAT, the sneaker?
turns.zh: 我是说，在担任社交雷达角色方面，有几个让我印象深刻的案例，因为我觉得这些创始人太棒了。我完全被说服了。他们的项目或许行不通，但基于这些创始人，我觉得绝对值得一试。事实也确实如此。我们还有几家最成功的公司，我对他们也有同样的感觉。你能感觉到他们对自己的项目了如指掌，深思熟虑过问题所在。他们解决问题不只是因为这类问题正当红、好玩刺激。有些问题很冷门，比如Parker Conrad申请Zenefits时，处理的是枯燥的HR和福利事务。但他深知现有体系的缺陷，并试图去改进。我特别喜欢这样的故事。还有一个例子，我成功说服其他合伙人投资了一家公司，叫GOAT，专门做运动鞋的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Okay. When Eddie and Daishin applied, they were not doing the sneaker company, they were doing this group sort of book-a-group-dinner at a restaurant with people you don't know as a way to meet new people. And for some reason, I loved the idea because I thought maybe it could be a secret dating, like a Trojan Horse for a dating sort of site. But I really loved the two founders. And one of the reasons, again, they had this passion about their idea, but they had had this cream puff company before that they had run, and they just told these stories about how hard it was and all this stuff. And I, for some reason, just thought, these are hustlers. These guys are scrappy. They're going to make this succeed. And they didn't make that company succeed, but they pivoted and made GOAT succeed and it's doing really, really well. And I remember that one I definitely had to convince... I mean, not that Paul, Robert and Trevor didn't like them, but I think they really didn't think the idea was that great or just sort of were meh. I was like, "We have to fund them."
turns.zh: 好的。Eddie和Daishin申请时，他们做的不是运动鞋公司，而是那个让陌生人在餐厅共进晚餐的平台。不知为何，我特别喜欢这个点子，因为我觉得这或许能变成秘密约会平台，像特洛伊木马般潜入交友网站。但我真的很欣赏那两位创始人。同样，他们对自己的想法充满热情，但他们之前经营过一家失败的公司，讲述了那些艰辛经历。不知为何，我觉得他们就是那种拼命三郎，坚韧不拔，注定会成功。虽然他们没能让之前的公司成功，但他们转型做GOAT，现在发展得非常好。记得当时我不得不说服其他人，比如Paul、Robert和Trevor。他们虽然不讨厌这两人，但觉得这个想法不怎么样，或者只是无感。我就坚持说，"我们必须投资他们。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love sharing these stories. If you have more to share, please keep throwing them out there. (00:28:27): So a few things I've noted so far, of things that you look for, and I think it's important to note this is very early stage evaluation where the founder and the team is, it's incredibly important, because the idea often shifts.
turns.zh: 我喜欢分享这些故事。如果你还有更多故事，欢迎随时分享。（00:28:27）：到目前为止，我注意到几个关键点。在评估创始人团队时，早期阶段的评估至关重要，因为创始人的想法往往会调整。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Oh, yeah. This is as early as it gets, Lenny.
turns.zh: 哦，对。就是这种最初的阶段，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Oftentimes, just an idea, I imagine.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过很多时候，我觉得这只是一种想法。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a few things, so far, things that you found to be really valuable to look for. One is this idea of just making shit happen, showing signs of being hustlers, just getting shit done, Obama O's, things like that. And then I think along the same lines, just passion for this idea and just like almost charisma. Is that how you think about it? Or is it just like...
turns.zh: 到目前为止，你发现的几个关键点都很重要。首先是那种能把事情搞定、展现出拼劲十足、能把事情做成的特质，比如奥巴马式的果断决策之类的。然后我觉得还有一种类似的特质，就是对这个想法充满热情，甚至近乎于魅力四射。你是这么看的吗？还是说……

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I hate using the word charisma because there are a lot of charismatic people who are full of baloney, and are just doing a startup because it's a cool thing to do now. And I wouldn't want anyone to get fooled by charisma. There has to be some substance behind that charisma. Of course, we all love talking to more charismatic people than less, and I've certainly talked to my fair share of totally uncharismatic people, but sometimes they're really good founders too. If they know what they're doing and care about the user and are fixing a problem that they have a deep connection to. So I don't want to say someone who's charismatic, but it definitely helps because, as you know, as a founder, you have to do a lot of sales and you have to recruit people and you have to convince investors to fund you and you have to convince users to use your product and all of this stuff. So it does help being charismatic, definitely.
turns.zh: 我不喜欢用“魅力”这个词，因为很多有魅力的人其实都是满嘴大话，只是因为现在创业很酷才参与其中。我不希望任何人被这种魅力蒙蔽。这种魅力背后必须有实质内容。当然，我们都更喜欢和有魅力的人交流，而我也确实接触过不少毫无魅力的人，但有时他们也是很优秀的创始人。只要他们清楚自己在做什么，关心用户，致力于解决自己深有共鸣的问题，那就足够了。所以我不想说有魅力的人一定好，但魅力确实有帮助，毕竟你知道，作为创始人，你需要做很多销售工作，招募人才，说服投资者投资你，吸引用户使用你的产品等等。所以有魅力确实有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So there's being super hustler, making shit happen. Domain expertise, something you've mentioned a few times. Just like having deep domain expertise in an area, and I think that's probably where they probably don't pivot oftentimes, where they've actually have experience in that specific problem.
turns.zh: 好的。所以首先是超级拼劲十足，能把事情搞定。然后你提到的领域专长，我已经提过几次了。就是在某个领域有深厚的专业知识，我觉得这可能是他们不轻易转向其他领域的原因，因为他们在那个特定问题上确实有经验。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: They might pivot a little bit, they might pivot a little in terms of the actual solution. They might be trying to solve a problem and the first attempt doesn't really work. I haven't mentioned earnestness though.
turns.zh: 他们可能会在解决方案上稍作调整。比如他们可能试图解决一个问题，但第一次尝试并不成功。不过我还没提到认真对待事务这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, do tell.
turns.zh: 哦，请说说吧。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Earnestness is one of the most important because earnest, sort of to me, is bucketed with authenticity. And to be a successful startup founder, you have to care so much about the problem you're trying to solve, the users you're serving and being earnest about it is so key to success. There are so many wannabe founders, so many people doing it because it's cool or they think this idea is cool, but they don't really, deep down, have what it takes. And I think we always try to fund earnest people.
turns.zh: 认真对待事务是最重要的一点，对我来说，认真和真诚是相通的。要成为成功的创业者，必须非常关心你试图解决的问题，关心你服务的用户，认真对待这些问题是成功的关键。有太多想成为创始人的人，有太多因为觉得酷或者觉得某个想法酷而参与其中的人，但他们其实没有真正的能力。我觉得我们总是倾向于资助认真的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does earnest look like in practice? And how does that come across?
turns.zh: 认真在实践中是什么样的？又该如何展现出来？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I think it means being sort of humble about... And if you get asked a question in the interview and you don't know the answer, they say, "I don't know the answer to that. I'd have to think about it." Or, "I don't know the answer. I've given it some thought and here's what I have come up with." And they're just honest about things, and they're not trying to do the whole smoke and mirrors thing, which we've definitely gotten people like that, that avoid the question or are doing it for the wrong reasons. (00:32:08): I remember there was one group that were 45-year-old men and they were building an app for teenagers in fashion. And I remember just thinking, we were asking them, "Why have you chosen teenagers in fashion?" And it was so clear that they thought they could make easy money, and it wasn't because they cared about fashion. It wasn't because, "Oh, I have a daughter who's really into fashion and I've seen this need." It was just like, they made up the idea. And that is not earnest, that is not authentic to me.
turns.zh: 我觉得这意味着要保持一定的谦逊……比如在面试中被问到一个问题时，你不知道答案，你可以说：“我不知道答案，我得考虑一下。”或者说：“我不知道答案，我思考了一下，下面是我的看法。”他们要诚实面对问题，而不是故作神秘。我们确实遇到过这样的人，他们回避问题或者出于错误的动机应对面试。（00:32:08）：我记得有个45岁的男性团队，他们在开发一款面向青少年的时尚应用。我记得当时我们问他们：“为什么选择青少年时尚领域？”很明显，他们认为这能轻松赚钱，并非出于对时尚的热爱。不是因为“我女儿对时尚很着迷，我发现了市场需求”。而是他们编造了一个想法。这对我来说太不真诚了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about it, so there's this earnestness you look for, also not being defensive. There's this also spectrum of confidence and people believing in what they're doing. Do you have any thoughts on just how to find that? What does that look like when they're too defensive versus they're just confident and then they know what they're talking about?
turns.zh: 你之前提到要寻找真诚，同时避免防御心理。自信和真诚之间也有个平衡，人们要对自己所做的事有信心。你有没有什么建议，如何判断一个人是否真诚？与过度防御相比，如何判断一个人只是自信且专业？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Confidence is good. You definitely want confidence. It's hard to... I think you can see it when you experience it. Like someone who's confident in answering your questions but isn't defensive, there's definitely a difference. And I don't know, this is why I'm saying it's sort of hard to articulate these things, but confidence means you can say, "I've thought about that and I don't know the answer." That's confidence. And they'll say, "But here's what I do to try to figure it out. Here are my plans to address that." Confidence, I should have put that upfront because that's very important, especially when it comes to fundraising, you cannot go into an investor meeting lacking confidence. You can come into YC's interview lacking confidence, but we will then help you in the next three months to gain more confidence. (00:33:58): And by the way, one of the things we do to help people gain more confidence is to make them believe that their startup is a great investment, to help them create a startup that truly is possibly going to make money or at least worth being a good bet. That's the thing, early stage, the best you can offer is like, "I might not succeed, but I'm definitely a good bet." And we help them with their product, we help them with their ideas, and we help them that, by demo day, they can get up on stage and legitimately say, "We're a good bet and here's why. Let me tell you about our idea." And so we definitely help with confidence.
turns.zh: 自信很重要。这很难用言语形容，但当你亲身经历时就能感受到。比如一个人自信地回答你的问题，但不显得防御，这两者有明显区别。我不知道，这就是为什么我觉得很难准确描述这些品质。但自信意味着你能说：“我考虑过这个问题，但确实不知道答案。”这就是自信。然后他们会说：“但我会采取这些措施来解决问题。以下是我的计划。”自信很重要，尤其是在融资环节，你不能带着不自信去见投资者。但你可以带着不自信参加YC的面试，然后我们会在接下来的三个月里帮助你提升自信。（00:33:58）：顺便说一句，我们帮助人们提升自信的方法之一，就是让他们相信自己的创业项目是一项很好的投资，帮助他们打造一个真正可能盈利或至少值得赌一把的创业公司。关键在于，早期阶段你能提供的最好承诺就是：“我可能不会成功，但我绝对值得一赌。”我们会帮助他们优化产品，完善创意，确保在Demo Day上，他们能自信地站在台上说：“我们值得一赌，理由如下。让我来跟你们讲讲我们的创意。”所以我们确实在提升自信方面下了很大功夫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. A couple other things you mentioned earlier, just to unpack a little bit. So being committed, something you look for, and co-founders getting along. In terms of committed, I imagine, these are very practical things. How are they actually going to stick to this? Are they actually excited to work on this? Maybe talk about that a little bit.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你之前提到的其他几个方面，稍微展开讲讲。比如团队成员是否要志同道合，共同为项目奋斗。关于志同道合，我想这应该是很实际的要求。他们要如何坚持下去？他们对这个项目是否充满热情？能多讲讲这方面吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: We all know how hard startups are, but I think you don't really know how hard it is until you actually do it. A lot of people would start a startup still having a job at Google or wherever, and they do it on the side. I do recommend, if people are just getting started and don't want to raise money yet, starting it on the side is a great way to get going, but at some point you have to commit, you have to burn the boat, because we found that founders who were still getting a paycheck and health insurance, once the going got tough, they did not quit their job. And you sort of need that desperation like, "I have to make this startup succeed because it's my job." Not like, "Oh, I'll just stay at Google." You need that. And we found that founders who weren't leaving their jobs, it was just not working out. Or that co-founder would always wind up leaving the company because they didn't want to actually leave their job. (00:36:01): And that's fine, there are people that can't leave their jobs for financial reasons. That's fine. You just shouldn't be starting a startup if you're not going to be prepared to leave your job. So that's the leaving of the job thing. And the co-founders getting along, oh my. I spent a lot of my time at Y Combinator when I was there all the time, full time, mediating co-founder disputes. And so many startups died or had near-death experiences because the co-founders didn't get along or broke up. It just happens all the time. And so that's why I think, during interviews, I was desperately trying to search for any clues that the co-founders didn't get along, or if they blatantly contradicted each other. But you could also tell if they were answering, finishing each other's sentences. (00:36:59): I love co-founders that have a history together; either they went to school together, they went to college together, work together, maybe they're siblings. Because when you have a long-term relationship, you trust each other and you know each other's weaknesses, and you're usually on the same page with your aspirations and everything. It's really scary when two founders get together just to start the startup and don't have any history. Massive red flag. Sometimes it works out like in the case of Dropbox, Drew and Arash both went to MIT, but I think they didn't know each other before they started Dropbox, and it worked out. But most of the time it doesn't.
turns.zh: 我们都知道创业之路有多艰难，但直到亲身经历，你才会真正领悟其中的不易。很多人在谷歌或其他公司工作时，同时兼职创业。我确实建议，如果刚起步且不想急于融资的人，可以先兼职试水。但到了一定阶段，你必须下定决心，全力以赴——就像我们发现，那些仍领着薪水、享受医保的创始人，一旦遇到难关，往往不愿辞职。而你需要那种迫切感：“我必须让这家创业公司成功，因为这是我的事业。”而不是心想：“哦，我就继续待在谷歌好了。” 这种决心至关重要。我们发现，那些不愿辞职的创始人，往往难以成功，或者合伙人最终会因分歧离队。（00:36:01）：这没什么问题。有些人因经济原因无法离职，这无可厚非。但如果你没有准备好放弃现职，就不该创办公司。这就是关于离职的问题。再说合伙人之间的磨合，天哪。我在Y Combinator全职工作时，大部分时间都在调解合伙人纠纷。许多创业公司因合伙人不合或分道扬镳而夭折，这种情况屡见不鲜。因此我在面试时总会留意合伙人是否合拍，或者他们是否公然互相反驳。但你也能从他们是否会接话、完成对方句子中看出端倪。（00:36:59）：我喜欢有共同经历的合伙人——比如同校、同读大学、共事，甚至是亲兄弟姐妹。因为长期关系能增进信任，了解彼此弱点，也更容易达成共同愿景。那些为了创业而临时组合、毫无前史的合伙人，风险极大。Dropbox的德鲁和阿拉什虽同是麻省理工校友，但据我所知他们相识于创业后，这才成功。但多数情况下都难逃厄运。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So we've talked about co-founders getting along, looking for defensiveness, domain expertise, the sign of making shit happen, earnestness. Is there anything else that we've missed that you look for in the founders that tell you maybe we should, maybe we shouldn't?
turns.zh: 我们已经谈过合伙人磨合、察觉防御心理、专业能力、成事的迹象和诚意，还有其他我们在创始人身上寻找的线索，比如他们是否值得投资？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Relentlessly resourceful. Paul wrote a whole essay on that. Every founder is different, I never try to say, "Oh, this person doesn't have this. I'm not going to fund them." You always have to... Everyone's different. But I mean, you're an investor. I'm curious, do any of these things surprise you or do you care about these things too?
turns.zh: 必须要足够善于资源整合。保罗专门写过一篇关于这点的文章。每个创始人不同，我从不轻易说：“哦，这个人没有这个特质，我就不投了。” 你总得……每个人都不一样。但作为投资者，我很好奇，你们是否也关注这些方面？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, absolutely not. Absolutely. And I actually try to avoid pre-seed and early stage because I'm not amazing at it, maybe. This is why I want to learn how to build my social radar skill.
turns.zh: 不，绝对不会。绝对需要。我其实尽量避开种子轮和早期阶段，因为我在这方面做得不好，或许吧。这就是我想学习如何培养社交洞察力的原因。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Oh gosh, okay.
turns.zh: 天哪，好吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Tough. It's so tough. It's like so few things actually work out.
turns.zh: 是的。太难了。真正成功的案例实在太少了。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Well, it's because you don't have a lot of data. If someone is just applying with an idea, you have very little data. You can look at where they went to college, what have they built in the past, that's always a great predictor of their ability. And so on the YC's application, we ask them, "What project have you worked on before?" Or whatever. But it's really hard to tell when you're the first investor.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是因为你没有足够的数据。如果有人只是带着一个想法来申请，那你能获取的数据就非常有限。你可以看看他们上过哪所大学，过去做过哪些项目，这通常能很好地预测他们的能力。在YC的申请流程中，我们会问他们：“你之前参与过哪些项目？”之类的问题。但当你是首位投资者时，确实很难判断他们的能力。

turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Vanta. When it comes to ensuring your company has top-notch security practices, things get complicated fast.
