That's V-A-N-T-A dot com slash Lenny. (00:40:00): When did you first notice that you had this social radar-ish skill and you're better at this than other people?
turns.zh: 本期节目由Vanta赞助。当需要确保公司拥有一流的安全实践时，事情很快就会变得复杂起来。现在，您可以通过单一平台Vanta评估风险、赢得客户信任，并实现SOC 2认证、ISO 27001认证、HIPAA合规等多项标准。Vanta市场领先的信任管理平台可帮助您持续监控合规情况，同时进行风险报告和追踪。此外，通过Vanta AI完成安全问卷调查，您可以节省大量时间。数千家全球公司正使用Vanta自动化证据收集、统一风险管理并简化安全审查流程。访问vanta.com/Lenny，即可获得1000美元优惠。（00:40:00）：你第一次注意到自己有这种社交雷达般的技能，比别人更擅长这方面，是什么时候呢？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Paul used to always call me Detective Livingston. Before I was a social radar, I was Detective Livingston. I cannot help myself noticing weird things, just dumb things, like if Paul had on a yellow T-shirt and then an hour later came in with a blue T-shirt, I'd be like, "Why do you have a blue T-shirt on?" I have to understand what happened in that hour where that T-shirt is different. Or people's what, their relationships, what drives them? I was always like this, and I think it goes back to my childhood. (00:40:44): I spent hours and hours on the phone with people, with my girlfriends, dissecting situations, and then all through high school, and college, I mean the amount of time we wasted discussing social matters with people, and boys, and things like that. It was just frightening how much time I wasted, but I just was genuinely interested in it. And what drives people and why did this happen? I don't know if I ever noticed I did this, but it was just, my point is, it's always been a part of me. And I definitely notice and having an aversion to phony people. I always have. I've never been one to fall for someone who's super phony and tried to have them as a friend or anything. I just can tell, and ugh, I hate it.
turns.zh: 保罗过去总是叫我“利文斯顿侦探”。在成为社交雷达之前，我就是“利文斯顿侦探”。我忍不住会注意到一些奇怪的事，甚至是一些愚蠢的事。比如，如果保罗今天穿了黄色T恤，几个小时后又换成蓝色的，我就会问：“你为什么穿蓝色T恤？”我必须弄清楚这一个小时里T恤为什么变了。或者是人们的关系，他们的动机是什么？我一直都是这样的，我觉得这可以追溯到我的童年。（00:40:44）：我花了无数时间和朋友们通电话，剖析各种情况，从高中到大学，我们浪费了大量时间讨论社交问题、谈论男孩之类的。回想起来真是令人震惊，但我就是对这些事情感兴趣。为什么人们会这样做？我不知道自己有没有意识到自己有这种行为，但这就是我的一部分。我确实注意到自己对虚伪的人很反感。我一直如此。我从不轻易被那些虚伪的人吸引，想和他们做朋友之类的。我能看出来，嗯，我讨厌这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you feel like it's almost all genetic or do you think there was something in your childhood that pushed you to be good at this?
turns.zh: 你觉得这几乎全是遗传因素，还是说童年时期的某些经历促使你擅长这方面？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I don't know. I really don't know. So this is why I think I'm going to be a bad guest, because I can't give a practical understanding. I mean, I don't really think... I can't say other people in my family are like that, and I can't say that it was part of my upbringing. I just notice these things. I don't know. I should be paying attention to other things, but I'm not, but I'm paying attention to this. I'll give you an example with you.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我真的不知道。所以这就是为什么我觉得自己可能不是个好嘉宾，因为我无法给出实用的见解。我是说，我不觉得……我不能说我家里其他人也这样，也不能说这是我成长环境的一部分。我只是注意到这些事情。我不知道。我本该关注其他事情的，但我没有，我却关注了这个。我给你举个例子吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: So I looked up your bio to read a little bit about you, and I loved the Dalton Caldwell Podcast. I listened to that.
turns.zh: 所以我查看了你的个人简介，了解了一些你的情况，我很喜欢《道尔顿·考德威尔播客》。我听过这个节目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fourth most popular of all time.
turns.zh: 史上第四受欢迎的人物。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Dalton's was?
turns.zh: 达尔顿的那个？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Oh, go Dalton. That's awesome. Yeah, it was really good. I learned a lot from it. I love listening to Dalton. But what I really want to know about you is, on the release that you sent, or on the instructions for this podcast, you said, "There might be some edge cases where your podcast isn't good enough to go out. We just want to warn you." And all I could think of is, what prompted that? There has to be a story of what prompted that. No one else would pay attention to that, but I'm just so curious. It's so weird. I'm just a weird person like this.
turns.zh: 哦，达尔顿真棒。太棒了。我从中学到了很多。我喜欢听达尔顿的节目。但我真正想问你的是，在你发送的发布说明或者这个播客的指南中，你提到“可能会有一些极端情况，比如你的播客不够优秀而无法发布。我们只是想提前提醒你。”我当时就想，到底是什么促使你这么说？这背后肯定有个故事。其他人可能不会在意，但我真的很好奇。这太奇怪了。我就是个奇怪的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, I did add that. There's a story, basically, it was just an episode that wasn't amazing and we didn't have that caveat in the prep beforehand, and it felt bad to tell the person.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实加了这段说明。基本上，就是有一期节目表现不佳，我们事前没有给出警示，最后不得不告诉对方，感觉挺不好意思的。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: See, I knew it. I knew that that had happened.
turns.zh: 看吧，我就知道。果然有这种事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly right. Is there kind of a way you've thought about honing this skill over time? Once you kind of got a sense, "Hey, people keep telling me I'm really good at this." Is there something you've done to help strengthen it?
turns.zh: 没错。你有没有想过如何不断磨练这项技能？当你意识到“大家都说我很擅长这个”之后，有没有采取什么措施来提升？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: No, but one of the things I do try to do is sort of reinforce. Sometimes I'll have a feeling about someone, maybe we fund them, maybe we don't. I'd sort of like to know what happens a few years later. I like to follow up. There definitely have been some situations where I haven't liked someone that we funded and it's taken 5 to 10 years before they failed. And in some cases, for a bad reason. Where I'll say, "Oh, thank God, I was right about that. I did have this feeling." Or, "I knew they'd be successful." Like the GOAT guys who I was saying before, there was definitely a period when Grubwithus, their first startup wasn't doing well, and they were starting, that maybe some people would've given up on them. And now I can say, "I was right about them. That feeling was right." (00:44:35): So I do try to sort of follow up with some of the really strong gut instincts that I had, to see if I was right. Often, when I have a gut instinct, it's like a negative thing. So we wind up not funding someone. So I really need to know if that person went on to be super successful. And I will answer your question right now, there's no one that I had a strong dislike for that I sort of said, "We should not fund them," that has gone on to be a super success. Thank God.
turns.zh: 没有。但我确实会努力巩固。有时候我对某个人有感觉，也许我们会资助他们，也许不会。我会想看看几年后他们会怎样。我喜欢跟进。有时候资助的项目一开始不顺利，五到十年后才失败。有些案例甚至是糟糕的结局。比如GOAT团队，我之前提到的那些人，他们的第一家创业公司Grubwithus一开始就不顺利，可能有些人当时就放弃了。现在我可以说：“我当时的感觉是对的。那种直觉是对的。” （00:44:35）所以我会去跟进那些强烈直觉，确认自己是否正确。通常，当我有这种直觉时，往往是负面的。所以我们最后决定不资助他们。但我真的需要知道这些人后来是否大获成功。我现在就回答你的问题，没有一个我强烈反对资助的人后来取得了巨大成功。谢天谢地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, interesting.
turns.zh: 哇，真有趣。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I mean, it doesn't happen all the time that I really put my foot down, but sometimes I have.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，并非每次我都坚决反对，但有时确实会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this feeling, is it like a visceral body thing for you? Or is it like intellectually, you notice, "Hey, this guy's interrupting her and this person doesn't..."?
turns.zh: 这种感觉，对你来说是本能的吗？还是说你会理性地注意到，“嘿，这个人在打断她，而那个人不……”？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: More intellectual. But it does come from inside. I don't know how to hone it. It has to come naturally. You have to have a natural interest in people. And so I'm sometimes not listening to all the words and I'm sort of just observing them, I don't know.
turns.zh: 更偏向理性。但它确实源自内心。不知道怎么磨练它。这得是天生的。你必须对人有天然的兴趣。所以有时我不会听清所有的话，只是观察他们，我也不知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you ever been tricked by someone where you didn't see something you should have seen? Is there anything there?
turns.zh: 你有没有被别人骗过，本该发现问题却没发现？有没有这类情况？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Oh, yeah, for sure. I can't really talk about the times I have been tricked just because I don't want to say anything really negative about people, but... Well, there was one example that I do feel comfortable sharing. Ilya Lichtenstein of MixRank. Do you know the guy that stole billions of dollars in Bitcoin from a crypto wallet? Do you not know this crazy, crazy story?
turns.zh: 哦，对啊，那是肯定的。我其实不太想谈那些被骗的经历，因为我不想对别人说些负面的话，不过……嗯，有个例子我倒是可以分享一下。MixRank的伊利亚·利希滕斯坦。你知道那个从加密钱包里偷走数十亿比特币的人吗？你不知道这个疯狂至极的故事吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please share.
turns.zh: 请分享一下。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I think he's in the joint now. He was definitely convicted of this, and his wife, and they stole billions of dollars. And I definitely don't remember thinking anything bad about him or thinking he could be that kind of person. So that definitely, there've been some doozies like that, where, did not see that one coming.
turns.zh: 我觉得他现在已经被关起来了。他肯定被判有罪了，他和他妻子一起偷了数十亿美元。我绝对不记得当时对他有什么不好的看法，也不认为他会是那种人。所以确实有过一些很离谱的事，让人完全想不到会发生这种情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. I think what's extraordinary about the fact that that happens rarely is that your interviews are 10 minutes long, and so you have very little time to actually find all these things. And plus, the actual product and the idea and growth strategy and all these things.
turns.zh: 天哪。我觉得这种情况很少发生的真正原因是，你的面试只有10分钟，所以根本没有足够的时间去发现所有这些问题。再加上产品本身、商业模式、增长策略等等这些方面。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Well, you find a lot can come in reading the application. That's a lot of legwork at the beginning. You read the application. But then the 10 minutes is kind of as long as you need, in most cases. Because we found when they were longer, like 20 minutes, you'd know in 10 minutes and be twiddling your thumbs trying to get through the interview for the next 10 minutes. So we kept them short so we could interview more people. But there have definitely been cases where we've interviewed people, accepted them, and then very soon afterward, we're sort of like, crestfallen like, "Oh, these people are very limp. What were we thinking?" Definitely, we've been tricked in that respect all the time. Or, "Oh gosh, they seem so impressive in the interview and now they're just posers who can't really do anything." Definitely, I'm tricked all the time in little ways. Or, I didn't notice two founders didn't get along and then one co-founder goes missing a week into the program or something crazy. There's all sorts of crazy stuff like that that happen.
turns.zh: 嗯，通过阅读申请材料能发现很多问题。那在初期需要做大量的基础工作。你得仔细阅读申请材料。但通常10分钟的面试时间已经足够了。因为我们发现如果面试时间太长，比如20分钟，你会在前10分钟就把该问的都问完了，然后剩下10分钟只能干坐着等下一个面试者。所以我们把时间控制得短一些，这样就能面试更多的人。但确实有过这样的情况，我们面试了某个人，录用了他，结果不久后我们就后悔不已，心想：“天哪，这些人太不靠谱了。我们当时怎么会看上他们？” 确实，我们经常在这种小细节上被骗。或者，“天哪，他们面试时表现得那么出色，结果却只不过是徒有其表，实际能力却很差。” 确实，我总是在一些小细节上被骗。又比如，我没注意到两个创始人合不来，然后其中一个创始人就消失了，项目才进行了一周，或者发生其他疯狂的事。这种离谱的事太多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think in the game you're playing, I would expect some things to slip through.
turns.zh: 我觉得在你所处的这个行业里，有些事情难免会被忽略。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that there's been kind of an operationalization of some of the things you used to look for in founders, now that you're not actually in the process. Is there a Jessica-as-a-service sort of thing? What kind of stuff have they built that looks for the sorts of things you used to look for in the interview process?
turns.zh: 你提到现在你不亲自参与面试了，所以对创始人的一些标准进行了流程化操作。是不是有类似“杰西卡式服务”之类的模式？他们开发了哪些工具来筛选面试时关注的那些特质？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: No, it's all just stuff in application that automatically flags certain things. I actually don't remember all of them, but it's just, all it is, is a, "Please pay attention to this, reader of the application." It's not, "This disqualifies anyone." It's, "Just please pay attention." And those are things like I mentioned, a really crazy equity structure, founders not quitting their job, things like that, that it's important that someone is voting on them and then interviewing them knows. Because I would often, some of the questions I'd ask at the end of the interview, I'd say, "It looks like you have 90% of the stock and your co-founder only has one. Can you tell us why that's the case?" And maybe they could make a case for it, who knows? But at least I'd ask. So the flags just say, "Pay attention to it."
turns.zh: 不是的，这些都只是应用程序中的自动标记功能。我其实记不清所有细节了，但核心意思就是，"请注意这一点，应用程序的读者们。" 这不是说"这会让任何人失去资格"，而是"请务必注意这些问题。" 比如我提到的那些问题——比如极其不合理的股权结构、创始人不辞职之类的，这些都需要有人在投票和面试时留意。比如我面试结束时会问，"看起来你持有90%的股份，而你的联合创始人只有1%。能解释下原因吗？" 也许他们能自圆其说，但至少我会追问。所以这些标记功能就是在提醒人们："请注意这些问题！"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So if we were to zoom out, in early stage investing, the main thing you need to get right and evaluate as the founder, the social radar skill that you've had from childhood is such an incredible advantage in doing this well, and you could basically say YC is what it is because of this unfair advantage that you all had in the early days. I'm guessing many people listening to this are like, "We need a Jessica on our team. We need to build this skill ourselves. We need to figure out how to integrate social radar into our process." I know you're going to hate this question, but just, do you have any advice for people that want to try to build the skill, get better at this, notice some of these things?
turns.zh: 太棒了。如果我们退一步看，在早期投资阶段，作为创始人，你需要正确评估的关键事项是什么？你童年时期就具备的社交洞察力，在这方面真是巨大的优势。可以说，YC之所以能成功，很大程度上是因为创始团队早期就拥有了这种不公平的优势。我猜很多听众会想："我们团队需要一个杰西卡（Jessica）这样的成员。我们得自己培养这种技能，必须想办法把社交洞察力融入我们的投资流程中。" 我知道你可能不爱回答这个问题，但还是想问：对于那些想提升这项技能的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I really think that our advantage was that my three co-founders were deeply technical people. And I think a lot of investors back then weren't, didn't have that background. And I think that that background really helped YC choose good founders. So I don't want to make it sound like it was that big of a deal, but advice? Advice for how to hone... I mean, I think just try to pay attention to subtle cues. If you really feel like, gosh, I'm so clueless about these things, try to just tell yourself, "Okay, I'm going in to evaluate these founders, evaluate this investment opportunity. I know I'm bad at these kind of judgments. I'm going to remember, do they seem like they get along?" Because there are no trick questions. I don't have any trick questions that you could ask, or it's just paying attention. Have a conversation. (00:51:26): Do they understand their product well? Are they defensive? Maybe have your own little checklist that you think about. You don't have to have it written down, but you think about, and then afterward, you spend some time thinking, were they defensive? When I asked them why this is better than the competitor, how did that go? Or ask them, maybe do have some questions, if you don't know how long they've known each other, ask them that question. "How did you two meet? Have you ever worked together before? How's it going?" Just be a little bit more conscious about asking these types of questions to reveal some key information for your investment decision.
turns.zh: 我真的认为我们的优势在于，我的三位联合创始人都是技术大牛。当时很多投资者没有这种背景，而这种技术背景确实帮助YC筛选出了优秀的创始人。所以我不想把这说得太神秘，但给点建议如何磨练这种技能……我的意思是，试着留意一些微妙的信号。如果你真觉得自己对这些东西一窍不通，那就告诉自己："好吧，我要去评估这些创始人，评估这个投资机会了。我知道自己在这类判断上很差劲。我要记住，他们相处融洽吗？" 因为没有什么陷阱题。我不会出什么刁钻问题，就是保持警觉。多交流。（00:51:26）他们是否对自己的产品了如指掌？他们是否防御性强？或许可以列个小清单。不用写下来，自己想想，然后回头再分析，他们有没有防御性强？当我问他们为什么比竞争对手更好时，结果如何？或者问他们，如果你不知道他们相识多久了，就问问这个问题。"你们怎么认识的？以前合作过吗？进展如何？" 在提问这些问题时多留个心眼，能为你的投资决策揭示关键信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was an awesome summary of a lot of the stuff we talked about. If anyone ever doubts that you are very good at this, Paul tweeted this quiz, the Reading the Mind in the Eyes quiz, that I took, it's incredibly hard. You basically see a bunch of eyes and you're supposed to judge their emotion, and it's really hard. And you got 36 out of 36, which blows my mind.
turns.zh: 你对我们讨论的很多内容做了精彩总结。如果有人怀疑你在这方面很在行的话，保罗发了这个"读懂眼中人心"测试，我做了，难度超高。你基本上要看一堆眼睛，判断他们的情绪，真的很难。我得了36分满分，这太让我惊讶了。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I did nail it. I do have to tell a funny story about this.
turns.zh: 我确实表现出色。不过关于这件事，我得讲个趣事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 拜托。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: So Paul, sort of late at night, and he emailed me, because I had gone to bed, but I had my thing, and he emailed me. He's like, "Check out this quiz. I got 25 out of 36. What can you get?" So I got my computer out because I was like, I have to beat Paul. And I did it, and it was really hard. They'd only show the eyes and then it would say, what is this person thinking? Are they happy, sad? But some of them were really hard to distinguish. Are they irritated or are they angry? It's kind of hard to tell the difference between irritated and angry. And I remember looking into these people's eyes saying, "What are they trying to communicate to me? Are they irritated with me or are they mad at me?" Kind of thing. (00:53:24): And as I went through, it would tell you if you got it correct. As I almost got to the end, I was like, "Oh my God, this is going to be a near-perfect score. I have to nail this." And when I got 36 out of 36, I was like, "Yes." And I told Paul, he tweeted it. We then, a week later, had this YC event in London, and I swear to God, about 10 people came up to me to talk about this eye quiz and how they had not done well, and what was my secret? It was very amusing. I never thought that anyone would think it was that interesting.
turns.zh: 有天深夜，保罗给我发邮件，因为我已经睡了，但我手机还开着。他说：“看看这个测试，我36道题答了25道。你能答几道？”我立马把电脑翻出来，心想：我一定要超过保罗。结果确实很难。测试只给出眼睛的图像，然后问：“这个人心里在想什么？是开心还是难过？”但有些表情实在难以分辨。比如“生气”和“恼火”之间的区别。记得我盯着那些人的眼睛，心里在想：“他们想对我传达什么？是对我不满，还是在生气？”之类的。（00:53:24）答题过程中，系统会提示你是否答对了。快到最后时，我紧张极了：“天哪，这次要拿满分了。必须成功。”最后36道题全答对，我兴奋地说：“太棒了。” 我告诉保罗后，他发了推特。一个星期后，我们在伦敦参加YC活动，天呐，至少有10个人过来找我聊这个眼部测试，说自己表现不佳，还问我秘诀是什么。真是太有趣了。我从没想过这事儿能这么受欢迎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that there's this thing that totally shows this skill you have that is better than everyone else. I took it, all my friends have taken it after that tweet, and the highest we've gotten is 31 of all the people I know.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种测试能充分展现你比别人更强的能力。自从那条推特后，我所有朋友都做过测试，目前我认识的人里最高分是31分。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think when people take it, we'll link to it, they're going to be like, "How can you get 36 out of 36? Impossible."
turns.zh: 我觉得大家做测试后会链接到这个页面，肯定会惊呼：“怎么可能36道全答对？太不可思议了。”

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: You have to look into their eyes and say, "What are they trying to tell me?" I hope you're not trying to tell me you're full of shit with your eyes.
turns.zh: 你得仔细观察他们的眼睛，判断他们想传达什么意思。希望他们别用眼睛告诉我你在胡说八道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm feeling despondent. Just kidding. That's one of the options. I'm like, "What does that even mean?"
turns.zh: 我现在感觉很沮丧。不过开玩笑的，这只是个选项。我当时就想：“这到底什么意思啊？”

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I know. Well, that's the other thing I told Paul, also the challenge is, you really have to understand what each feeling, what that word means. He's like, "Oh, that didn't even occur to me." Because he's such a word person and knows the exact definition of every single word. But I thought some people will struggle understanding the complexities of the emotion.
turns.zh: 我知道。嗯，这也是我跟保罗说过的另一件事。挑战在于，你必须真正理解每种情绪、每个词的含义。他当时说：“哦，我都没想到这一点。”因为他对词汇特别敏感，每个词的准确定义都烂熟于心。但我觉得有些人可能很难理解情绪的复杂性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With the words, I almost felt like I had to do what you did where just like, "What does this word feel like when I'm reading it? Despondent, let's see if these eyes are despondent." I love that trick you shared. So basically you looked at the eyes and you're like, "What is this person trying to tell me?"
turns.zh: 关于这些词汇，我几乎觉得自己得像你那样做——比如，“当我读到‘沮丧’这个词时，它给人的感觉是怎样的？看看这双眼睛有没有沮丧的感觉。” 我喜欢你分享的这个技巧。基本上就是看着对方的眼睛，然后想：“这个人想告诉我什么？”

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Yeah, that's the best I could do.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也只能做到这样了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So we're going to link to that quiz. I'm curious what people, if you take it, please leave your score in the comments, see if anyone can get anywhere near Jessica's score. Okay. So speaking of social radar-ing, you have a podcast called The Social Radars.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会把这个测试的链接放在节目里。我很好奇，如果你们参加测试的话，能不能在评论里留下自己的得分，看看有没有人能接近杰西卡的分数。好了。说到社交洞察力，你有个播客叫《社交洞察力》。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about it.
turns.zh: 咱们来聊聊吧。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Yes, okay.
turns.zh: 是的，好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First of all, just why did you decide to start a podcast? There's a lot of podcasts in the world. What made you decide to start one?
turns.zh: 首先，你为什么决定开办播客呢？世界上有很多播客。是什么促使你决定创办一个呢？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Well, I'm really excited that you're asking that question because no one has ever asked me about The Social Radars. Yes, I mean, it's pretty new, but we launched last year. I decided to start The Social Radars because I live off in the English countryside, not really as connected as I'd like to be with Silicon Valley, partly by choice, but I do miss it a lot. And I was finding that as I was catching up with YC alumni that would come visit or I'd see, I just loved the conversations we were having, and I missed that. I missed that connection with these people, and sort of sharing their stories of triumph and failure in some cases, but mostly triumph. At the same time, I became obsessed with this podcast called SmartLess. Have you ever heard of it?
turns.zh: 嗯，我真的很高兴你能问这个问题，因为从来没有人问过我关于《社交雷达》的事。是的，我知道这个播客才刚起步，但我们去年就上线了。我决定创办《社交雷达》，是因为我住在英国乡村，这里和硅谷的联系不像我希望的那样紧密，部分是出于个人选择，但我确实很怀念那里。当我和来访的YC校友聊天，或者在社交场合见到他们时，我发现我们之间的对话非常有趣，我很怀念那种联系——分享他们的成功与失败故事（当然大多是成功）。与此同时，我迷上了《SmartLess》这个播客。你听过吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've heard of it, haven't listened.
turns.zh: 听说过，但没听过。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Okay. So just for the listeners, it is a podcast hosted by three actors; Jason Bateman, Will Arnett and Sean Hayes. And they invite Hollywood people, actors, directors, musicians, sometimes athletes, on the show. And the thing is, one person, one of the hosts invites the guests, the other two don't know. So there's no preparation, and it's the most fascinating thing. I love movies and I love television, and I can tell you another weird eccentric gift of mine is I remember every name in Hollywood and know all their children and all this stuff because I've been reading People Magazine since I was 13. So I loved, you'd learn so much about the actors as people because they weren't talking from a script or their media messages for promoting a movie. It was like just genuine conversations. Most of the time these actors knew the people and were friends, and I just found it fascinating. I could not stop. (00:57:25): And I thought there should be a really informal conversation like this with startup founders so people could understand the people behind the startups. And it's not too scripted and not too, maybe, I don't want to say professional, because I hope it's professional sounding, but it's very conversational and authentic. I was trying to mimic that a little bit. I convinced my colleague and friend, Carolynn Levy, who of course has a full-time job being one of the amazing lawyers within YC, and she's super busy. I convinced her to do it with me so I could have a partner in crime. And then we just started and I said, "We'll do a few episodes, see how it goes, and we'll keep going if it's fun." And I have had so much fun catching up with all the people I've interviewed. At this point, I forget how many podcasts I've even done, but maybe-
turns.zh: 好的。给听众介绍一下，这个播客由三位演员主持：杰森·贝特曼、威尔·阿奈特和肖恩·海斯。他们邀请好莱坞人士——演员、导演、音乐家，有时是运动员——上节目。关键是，其中一位主持人邀请嘉宾，其他两位主持人事先不知道嘉宾是谁。所以没有准备时间，这才是最迷人的。我热爱电影和电视，我可以告诉你，我还有个奇怪的癖好——从13岁起我就开始读《人物》杂志，所以我记得好莱坞每个人的名字、他们的孩子之类的。所以我很喜欢通过这个播客了解演员们作为个体的一面，因为他们不是在照着剧本说话，也不是为了宣传电影而塑造的形象。这就像真诚的对话。大多数情况下，这些演员彼此相识、是朋友，我觉得这很吸引人。我根本停不下来。（00:57:25）然后我想，应该有一个和创业者们这样非正式的对话，这样人们就能了解创业者背后的故事了。不会太刻意，不太专业——虽然我希望它听起来专业，但更像是随意的交流，真实自然。我试着模仿那种风格。我说服了我的同事兼好友卡罗琳·利维，她在YC担任律师，工作非常忙碌。我说服她和我一起做，这样我就能有个搭档了。然后我们就开始了，说"先做几期看看效果，如果有趣就继续下去。"和所有我采访过的人聊天都非常开心。我现在都忘了自己做了多少期播客了，但可能——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think about 27-ish.
turns.zh: 我觉得大概27期左右。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: 27 that have launched yet, and there's a few coming out. Season three, we're still in the middle of that, and still editing some and doing some. But it's been so much fun and I love it, and I hope that people enjoy listening. I hope I'm not just working this really small corner of the room. I hope people enjoy unstructured conversations. But people open up to me though, because what I copied from SmartLess that I liked, they'd say, "Hey, remember when we were at that Oscars party and this happened..." Because they had that relationship with the people they're interviewing, in a lot of cases, I feel like I've had that with a lot of people I'm interviewing and I could say, "Hey, Brian, remember when you interviewed and brought the cereal boxes?" And he could tell, he shared that story. I don't think I knew it before then that they were on the 101 and the phone went out, the reception went out before Paul said that they were accepted. So I learn a lot, and it's really just fascinating to me.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，已经有27期播客上线了，还有几期即将推出。第三季我们仍在制作中，目前仍在剪辑和进行相关工作。整个过程非常有趣，我很享受这个过程，也希望听众们能喜欢。我不希望自己只是在播客这个小角落里耕耘。我希望人们能喜欢这种非结构化的对话。不过人们确实对我敞开心扉——比如我从SmartLess节目中借鉴的部分，他们会说：“嘿，还记得我们在奥斯卡派对上发生的那件事吗？”因为他们和受访者之间建立了深厚的联系。在很多情况下，我也和采访对象产生了共鸣。比如我可以说：“嘿，布莱恩，还记得你采访时带上麦片盒子的那次吗？”他立刻就想起那件事，还分享了那个故事。我之前并不知道他在101号公路上时手机没信号，保罗宣布他们项目被接受前信号中断了。所以我学到了很多东西，这对我来说真是太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, it's an awesome podcast, I've been listening. I'm going to just read some of the guests that you've had on, just so people get a sense of who you're interviewing. So you actually just had Paul Graham on the podcast. He does very few podcast episodes. So that's an unfair advantage you have there. Patrick and John Collison, Brian Chesky, you mentioned Brian Armstrong, Emmett Shear, Tony Xu, like epic people.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是一个很棒的播客，我一直在听。我想读一些你邀请过的嘉宾名单，让大家对你的采访对象有个概念。比如你刚邀请了保罗·格雷厄姆，他很少做播客节目。这真是你占了先机啊。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Emmett Shear, by the way, the week after he was named OpenAI CEO for like 72 hours, that one launched. I was like, I could not have planned that timing better.
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，埃米特·希尔被任命为OpenAI首席执行官一周后，他的播客就上线了。我当时就想，我真是安排得再巧不过了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an episode you'd recommend people start with if they were start to explore your podcast and get into it?
turns.zh: 如果有人想开始探索你的播客并逐渐沉浸其中，有哪一期你会推荐他们从头听起？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Honestly, I truly believe this, I'm not BS-ing you, I think they're all really, really good, and there's so many interesting takeaways from every single one. If I were coming to it for the first time, I'd probably choose, I'd look at the guests and say, "Who am I interested in? Have I stayed at an Airbnb and I want to learn more about that?" Or, "Do I use Reddit?" Just see who the guests are and start with someone you're kind of interested in, and I guarantee you'll learn more about this person.
turns.zh: 说实话，我真心觉得每一期都非常精彩，每一期都有很多有趣的收获。如果我第一次接触这个播客，我可能会先看看嘉宾名单，问自己：“我对谁感兴趣？我是否住过Airbnb，想了解更多相关内容？”或者，“我是否使用Reddit？”只要看看嘉宾是谁，选一个你感兴趣的人开始听，我保证你会对这个人有更深入的了解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So across the podcast episodes you've done, I hate when people ask me this question, but I'm going to ask you this question. Is there any big lessons you've learned, any stories that have stuck with you? Any takeaways so far from interviewing all these incredibly successful founders and people?
turns.zh: 在你制作的播客节目中，我讨厌别人问我这个问题，但我还是要问你一个问题。在采访了这么多极其成功的创始人和人士后，你有没有学到什么重要经验，有没有印象深刻的故事？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: My God, I love that question. I don't hate that question.
turns.zh: 天哪，我超爱这个问题。我一点都不讨厌这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I'm glad.
turns.zh: 好的，我很高兴。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I could talk for an hour just on... I want to learn from you as an expert podcaster, because I'm still a noob here. What I've learned the hard way, and you probably will nod your head when I say this, is that I talk way too much. I'm a huge windbag and I hate... I don't notice it now when I'm just talking to you and going off and talking, talking, talking. But when I'm editing the podcast and I'm listening to myself ask a question in 20 sentences when I could ask it in two. So I've really had to train myself to keep things short. You want regular short dialogue, you know this, but you also have to interrupt guests if they're going off too much. So the talking of the hosts should be frequent but short. That's the lesson that I've learned.
turns.zh: 我可以谈上一个小时……我想向你这样的播客专家学习，因为我在这方面还是个新手。我吃了不少苦头才明白（相信你听我说这些时会点头），我说话太多了。我是个话痨，讨厌……现在和你们聊天时我没注意到自己一直在说个不停。但编辑播客时，听自己用20句话才能问完的问题，实在太烦了。所以我必须训练自己简洁明了。你知道，日常对话要简洁，但遇到嘉宾过于冗长时也要打断他们。所以主持人要频繁发言但保持简短。这就是我学到的教训。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Totally agree.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: In terms of content, every single episode is a gem in its own right, and there aren't massive lessons because they're all sort of specific to that person, and I never know exactly which direction we're going to go in when we get into things. But it was interesting. There were definitely some themes with Adora Cheung and Tony Xu of DoorDash where they said they really made a mistake early on scaling into different cities before they had nailed the original city. And that's an important lesson. There's lessons for everyone, I think. In addition to really getting to know these founders, their personal side of their personality, there's some great lessons that they all tell.
turns.zh: 在内容方面，每一期播客都是独立的精品，虽然没有宏大的普遍启示，因为每个嘉宾的故事都各具特色，我也不知道每次访谈会走向何方。但确实很有意思。比如和Adora Cheung、DoorDash的Tony Xu对谈时，他们提到早期在未完善原有城市业务前就扩展到其他城市是个错误。这是个重要教训。我觉得每个人都能从中汲取经验。除了深入了解这些创始人及其个性特质，他们分享的宝贵经验也令人受益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love these lessons. Is there anything else you've learned about interviewing? That's something I'm always trying to get better at. I love this point you made. I say the same thing to every podcaster. You talk too much as a host, you should let the guest talk. Just ask the question and let them talk. Is there anything else that you've learned about just how to interview more effectively?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这些启发。采访方面你还有什么心得？这正是我一直在努力提升的技能。你提到主持人说话太多，要让嘉宾畅谈。这点我深有同感。我每次都对播客嘉宾说：你别多说，该问问题时就问，让他们自己说。还有什么高效采访的技巧吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Remember, I've been interviewing people since YC started because I was working on Founders at Work simultaneously when we started YC, and so that was a collection of interviews. And back then, I can't say I was that good at it. I've gotten much better. And then I've since gone, I used to do a lot of interviews at startup school on stage with people, and now the podcast. I think one thing that is that the guests trust me. They trust that I'm not going to try to have a gotcha moment. I'm not trying to lure them into saying anything controversial. Do I love it when they say something that hasn't been said before? Yes. But I'm not trying to trick them. (01:03:37): And just like you, I tell them, "You will have a chance to review this before it goes public." And I think that disarms people and they say, "Okay, I can open up because I know if I regret saying something, it's not like talking to a reporter who's going to publish it." I care about them. I care about making them look good, and I'd never want to betray their trust, and they know that. So that's part of it too. For me, with the podcast, I have some questions that I do ahead of time just so I have something down, but I also just let the conversation go where it's going, and we get into some random tangents that I find are really fascinating.
turns.zh: 记得吗？自从YC启动以来我就开始采访人，因为我们创办YC时我同时在做《Founders at Work》系列访谈。当时我承认自己水平不算高，但现在进步了很多。后来我在创业学校舞台上采访过许多人，现在则专注播客。我觉得关键是嘉宾信任我。他们知道我不会故意设圈套引他们说出有争议的话。我喜欢他们说出前所未闻的观点吗？当然。但我不是故意套话。（01:03:37）和你们一样，我会提前告知他们：“播出前有机会审核内容。”这样能消除他们的顾虑，他们会说：“好的，我可以畅谈了，因为知道即使说错了也不像面对记者会被报道出去。”我关心他们，重视他们的形象绝不会背叛他们的信任。他们也明白这一点。所以这也是关键所在。对我来说，播客部分我会提前准备一些问题，但也会顺着访谈自然发展，有时会聊到一些意想不到的有趣话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story that stand out to you just that sticks with you from the interviews that just like, "Wow, that was such an incredible story someone shared with me," or, "a lesson learnt."?
turns.zh: 是否有某个采访故事令你印象深刻，让你久久难忘？比如，"哇，那个人分享的故事真是太不可思议了"，或者"从中得到了一课"？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: The podcast that really sticks with me is the Parker Conrad episode, of Rippling, but we spent a lot of time on Zenefits because if you didn't follow that story years ago, the press annihilated him. And in talking to him, I learned why. There was a smear campaign paid for by someone still at Zenefits. There were legal threats made to force him to sign this legal document that would allow them to have a non-compete in California so that he couldn't another company, basically making his life miserable, disparaging him. Stories planted in the press. And I had him come on and I had him tell what really happened. (01:05:29): And even I, who have seen so much shit behind the scenes with startups in Silicon Valley over the years, stuff you just couldn't believe. This was unbelievable. And the thing that really sticks with me is that no reporter ever, maybe no reporters listened to it, but no one said, "Hey, I got that wrong years ago. I shouldn't have written that. That wasn't true. Let me set the record straight." So he doesn't care. Parker's moved on, he's successful with Rippling, he doesn't think about this stuff. But I do. I care about justice. And it was a horrible thing that was done to him and it affected his health, it affected his life, and I just am glad to have sort of been a conduit to set the record straight.
turns.zh: 有一期播客让我印象特别深刻，是《Rippling》节目中关于帕克·康拉德（Parker Conrad）的访谈。但我们在节目中花了很多时间讨论Zenefits公司的情况。要是你几年前没关注过那起事件，就会知道媒体把他批得体无完肤。和他交谈后，我才明白原因——Zenefits公司里至今仍有高管花钱策划了针对他的抹黑活动。他们还用法律威胁迫使他签署协议，要求他在加州遵守竞业禁止条款，这样他就无法创办其他公司。他们处处给他使绊子，向媒体散播不实消息。我邀请他上节目，让他讲述真实经历。（01:05:29）即便我多年来在硅谷见过太多创业圈背后的黑幕，种种离谱行径，但这次事件仍令人震惊。最让我难忘的是，媒体从未反思过自己的错误。或许没有记者听过这期节目，但没人站出来说：“嘿，我多年前报道有误，应该纠正错误。”这太冷漠了。帕克已经向前看，在Rippling公司取得成功，他不再纠结于这些过往。但我却始终牵挂着正义。这场针对他的恶意攻击影响了他的健康和生活，我很庆幸能通过节目为他洗清冤屈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome episode maybe for people to start with if they want to check out the podcast. And then generally, I just love this rise of ways for tech people to share their story without this drive to create clicks and create gotcha moments and things like that. Just this, I think people call it techno optimism, this idea of just like tech is great, technology is doing great things for us, let's just tell these stories in a really positive way versus look at all the harm they're causing, technology stop, slow it down.
turns.zh: 这期节目很棒，如果大家想入门播客，或许可以从这期开始。总的来说，我特别喜欢科技人士能以更正面、积极的方式分享经历，而非为了博眼球、制造戏剧性冲突。比如“科技乐观主义”，即科技本质上是好的，正在为人类创造美好，大家应该以积极视角讲述这些故事，而非只关注其负面影响。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: And I just want to have conversations that I personally find interesting. I'm very selfish about it, Lenny. As long as I have an interesting conversation, I tell Carolyn this all the time, as long as we have 20 listeners, that's all I need. 20 really interested listeners, we'll keep doing it.
turns.zh: 我只想聊自己感兴趣的话题。我很自私，莱尼。只要能进行有趣的对话，我就常和卡罗琳说——只要有20个听众，我就能坚持下去。20个真正感兴趣的听众，我们就继续做下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that attitude. I wish I had that same feeling. What I look for is, is it growing? That's the thing. I'm like, is it growing at least? If it's growing, no matter what it is, I'm feeling good.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种态度。真希望自己也能有同感。关键在于，是否在不断成长？我总在想，至少得在成长吧？只要在成长，无论做什么，我都会感觉良好。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I need to be a little bit more like that. I don't know any of my statistics. What statistic, you tell me as an experience podcaster, what statistics should I have taped up to my mirror every day and track?
turns.zh: 我需要更像他一点。我对自己的数据一无所知。作为经验丰富的播客主，你能给我点建议吗？我该把哪些数据贴在镜子上，每天追踪？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's the correct one and there's a simple one that I look at, which is just downloads of the episode. It's the most basic one you see everywhere. And downloads is a weird one because they might download and not listen to it, but that's just the one that podcast platforms tell you how many people have downloaded it. And that's the one that just tells you generally, are people listening? Are people continuing to listen? Did they remove it from their phone? In theory, you should be looking at retention like how many people are finishing the podcast episode?
turns.zh: 有一份正确的数据，还有一份我关注的简单数据，那就是剧集的下载量。这是最基础的数据，到处都能看到。而下载量这项数据有点奇怪，因为人们可能下载了却不听，但播客平台会告知你有多少人下载了它。这项数据能大致反映听众的参与度：他们是否听完了整集？是否持续收听？又或者他们把它从手机里删掉了？理论上，你应该关注用户完成收听的数据，比如有多少人听完了整个播客剧集？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Can you tell that though? I thought these platforms don't share that with you.
turns.zh: 但你能分辨出来吗？我觉得这些平台不会主动分享这些数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Some do, some do. Spotify gives you some of that. Apple, gives you. The worst part about podcasting is the analytics are extremely bad and inconsistent, but there are some of those stats. The other one, okay, here's one to pay attention to, is number of subscribers on the different platforms, people that follow you. That actually is a really important metric to watch.
turns.zh: 有些平台会，有些不会。Spotify会提供部分数据，苹果平台也一样。播客分析数据极其糟糕且不一致，但还是有一些关键指标。比如不同平台的订阅用户数量（关注你的人），这才是真正值得关注的数据。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Number of subscribers, okay. One thing I also, this is just my personality, I can't bring myself to do what I want to, is ask people if you like The Social Radars, please subscribe and leave a rating and a review. I would do anything to have people leave rating and reviews.
turns.zh: 订阅用户数量，对。我也有点纠结，因为我实在不忍心去做我想做的事——请听众订阅并留下评分和评论。我愿意用任何方法让人们留下评分和评论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you're listening and you either checking out the podcast or you're already a listener, please leave a rating and a review and subscribe and follow.
turns.zh: 如果你正在收听，或者已经是听众，请留下评分和评论，订阅并关注。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Thank you. Can I ask you a question about podcasting really quickly?
turns.zh: 谢谢。我能快速问你一个关于播客的问题吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sure, let's do it.
turns.zh: 当然，咱们接着聊。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: When you do a podcast, after you hang up with a person, can you tell, do you have a gut instinct like, "Oh, that was a really great "?
turns.zh: 做播客后，挂掉电话后，你能感觉到吗？有没有种直觉：“哇，这个人太棒了！”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting is, the ones that I sometimes think, holy moly, that was incredible, don't do as well as I would think. And sometimes ones I think didn't go amazing, actually do a lot better than I think. And I think there's a difference between the energy and the fun of it versus the content and the interesting value of the actual conversation. And so sometimes you feel like that was so fun, so good, I loved it, but people are like, "Nah, I didn't learn anything." So those are interesting. That's something I've learned.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，我有时觉得“天哪，太棒了！”的人，反而没我想象的那么受欢迎。有时我觉得表现平平的，反倒比我预期的要好得多。我觉得这和对话的活力与趣味性，以及实际内容的价值有区别。有时你觉得太有趣、太棒了，但听众却说：“不，我没学到什么东西。”所以这很耐人寻味。这也是我学到的一点。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Okay. Yeah, because people come to yours expecting to learn things. Now I'm a little nervous, I'm going to get axed because I'm not teaching them anything valuable.
turns.zh: 好的。是啊，因为听众来听播客是希望能学到东西的。现在我有点紧张，怕被解雇，因为我没教给他们任何有价值的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're so modest. This was incredible. I think we've taught people a lot of really important and really actionable things and I know you don't think you did, but you did. And with that, we've covered a ton of ground. We've talked through every single thing that I was hoping we talked through. Is there anything else you wanted to share or maybe leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 你太谦虚了。这次太棒了。我觉得我们教给听众很多真正重要、切实可行的知识，我知道你不这么认为，但确实如此。说到这儿，我们已经聊了很多。我希望聊到的每个话题都涉及到了。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享或留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: No, I mean, honestly I can't think of... I think I windbagged enough.
turns.zh: 没有了，说实话我想不到什么了……我已经啰嗦得够多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This was incredible. You talked exactly the right amount of time. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你讲话的时长恰到好处。接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Ready as I'll ever be.
turns.zh: 我已经准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. First question, what are two or three books that you recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好。第一个问题，你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Well, I definitely would recommend my first, second and third books would all be P.G. Wodehouse books. Do you know him as an author?
turns.zh: 嗯，我肯定会推荐我的第一本、第二本和第三本——都是P.G.沃德豪斯的书。你听说过他吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Ask Jeeves. Okay, so he was an old school author and he wrote the Ask Jeeves books about the Butler and Bertie Wooster.
turns.zh: 去问问维基百科吧。好吧，他是一位老派作家，写过关于巴特勒和伯蒂·伍斯特的"问杰夫斯"系列书籍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not the search engine.
turns.zh: 不是那个搜索引擎。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: They're so funny and fabulously written. His use of words makes me laugh so hard. And so I would specifically recommend the starter books that... He wrote tons of books and he lived till he was like a hundred. Start with Very Good, Jeeves or Right ho, Jeeves, Carry On, Jeeves. Those three are really good books. And then I tend to read, so Paul's the big reader in the family, he reads riveting books on Roman grains and anything that has to do with medieval history. I tend to read biographies of people, especially musicians, especially English musicians, strangely. And so I've recommended, to a lot of people, if you really want a good autobiography, because I sometimes hate autobiographies because I feel like people hold back and don't really share everything. Keith Richards, his autobiography called Life, is really good if you're a fan of the Rolling Stones at all. That was really good. (01:12:04): And then I recently read Barbra Streisand's biography called, I think it's called, My Name is Barbra something, and I kept thinking as I was reading this, every female founder should read this book. And you're looking at me like that's so random, but it's because she was such a success within this totally male-dominated world of Hollywood and just treated like garbage and dismissed and called a diva when she was very particular about something. Whereas, a man would be called a great director and she was called a diva, and I felt like every woman should just read this to inspire them. It was such a great book. Long, but very good.
turns.zh: 那些书太有趣了，写得极为精彩。他用词的幽默感让我笑得不行。具体来说，我会推荐他的入门书籍……他写了大量书籍，一直活到一百多岁。可以从《非常好》《问杰夫斯》或《好的，杰夫斯》开始。这三本都非常棒。然后我自己比较爱阅读——保罗是家里的大书虫，他读关于罗马谷物和中世纪历史的书。我则喜欢读名人传记，尤其是英国音乐家的，奇怪的是。还有，我向很多人推荐过，如果你想读一部好的自传，因为有时我不太喜欢自传，觉得作者有所保留没全盘托出。比如基思·理查兹的《生活》——如果你喜欢滚石乐队的话，这本书很棒。（01:12:04）最近我读了芭芭拉·史翠珊的传记，好像叫《我的名字叫芭芭拉》之类的，读的时候一直在想，每个女性创业者都应该读这本书。你可能会觉得这很随意，但正是因为她在好莱坞这个男性主导的世界里取得了成功，却被视为异类、被贬低、被称为天后，而当一个男人对某件事有自己的坚持时，就会被称为伟大导演。我觉得每个女性都应该读这本书，获取启发。内容很长，读起来却很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible recommendations. Next question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 太棒了。下一个问题，你最近有没有喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I don't tend to watch recent movies. I watch old school movies from the 50s through the 90s and stuff. My favorite new TV show, just off the top of my head right now, is Clarkson's Farm. Have you heard of that, on Amazon?
turns.zh: 我不太看新片。我看50到90年代的老片子。最近喜欢的电视节目，突然想到的是《克拉克森的农场》。你听说过吗？亚马逊上能看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nope.
turns.zh: 没听过。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Jeremy Clarkson, he's in the show called Top Gear. I don't watch that. But he lives out in the English countryside. He has a farm, and he decided that he'd farm it. And the whole show is about him getting into this business that he knows nothing about, everything goes wrong, but it is hysterical and heartbreaking at the same time. I've learned so much about England and about where I live and the crops that are grown, and how hard it is for farmers. He's really shone a light on the difficulty of being a farmer these days and it's fabulous. Clarkson's Farm. And it has some bad language in it, but I do recommend that kids watch it, because it's just a good show to watch as a family if you can deal with a little foul language. The Brits drop a lot of F-bombs.
turns.zh: 杰里米·克拉克森，他参与了一档叫《巅峰拍档》的节目。我不怎么看那档节目。不过他住在英格兰的乡下。他有座农场，决定亲自经营。这档节目全是关于他涉足一个完全陌生的领域，诸事不顺，但又令人捧腹又心碎的经历。我对英格兰、自己生活的地区以及当地农作物有了深刻认识，也深知农民的艰辛。他真实地揭示了当今农民的困境，真是太棒了。《克拉克森的农场》这档节目里有一些粗俗语言，但我还是推荐孩子们观看，因为只要能接受那些脏话，这确实是一档适合全家一起看的精彩节目。英国人动不动就爆粗口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, share with people, find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 你有没有特别钟爱的座右铭，经常回味、与人分享、在工作或生活中觉得很有用的？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: It's so boring, but I always try to treat people the way I'd like to be treated myself, really, is fundamental life lesson.
turns.zh: 这听起来挺无聊的，但我总是努力以希望被他人以同样的方式对待的标准来对待他人。这确实是人生最基本的准则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like boring but so powerful and important. And I try to live that same way. And I think it's a good reminder to people, sometimes the most, I think it was Michael Pollan had said that, "Cliches are cliches because they're so true." They're so true, we're tired of hearing it. Sometimes it's important to be reminded of them. Who's most influenced you in your career? Who do you think of when you're like, this person's really had the most influence on me?
turns.zh: 虽然听起来无聊，但它又极其有力且重要。我努力践行这一理念。有时我会想起迈克尔·波伦的话：“陈词滥调之所以成为陈词滥调，正是因为它们太真实了。” 它们太真实了，以至于我们听腻了。但有时被提醒一下也很重要。在你的职业生涯中，谁对你影响最大？当你回想时，谁对你的影响最深？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: In my career, I definitely have to say my husband, Paul Graham. I've just learned so much from him over the years, and he's such a good person and I think people who know him, all know that he is. It's just, he has such a big online personality either through Twitter or through his essays. And so he has a lot of people that don't like him, because he also speaks what he believes. And he is not afraid to say anything if he believes it's true and needs to be said. Whereas, I'm the exact opposite. I'm like, "Oh, I'm not going near that. I'm not touching that with a ten-foot pole. I don't even want to get in someone's crosshairs or fight with someone." And I admire that so much. There's so much that he's done with Y Combinator and just in our personal life that is just so admirable and I've really learned a lot from him. (01:15:53): It's such a boring thing to learn from your husband, but at the same time, I'm going to extend this, I'm going to windbag a little bit longer. I have learned so much from the founders that we funded. Some of them are just incredible people and have been through so much and survived so much and built these amazing companies that I couldn't have even imagined when we funded them, that these companies would be as successful as they are, and they're all, so many of them, are just great people. And they now teach me things, honestly. Like Brian Chesky teaches me things. The student has become the master. He knows so much more about me and running a business, and I often will go to him for advice. And so I'm really lucky to be surrounded by so many smart people in the startup world, because as a startup nerd, I could talk about startups and think about them all the time, and it's so great to have all these people around sort of lifting me up.
turns.zh: 在我的职业生涯中，毫无疑问是我的丈夫保罗·格雷厄姆。这些年来我从他身上学到了太多东西。他是个非常好的人，我认识他的人都知道这一点。他在推特或文章中展现出极强的网络人格，所以招来不少反感。但他从不畏惧说出真相，只要他认为某事真实且必须说出口。相比之下，我完全相反。我会说：“哦，我绝对不会碰那样的事情。我绝对不会去招惹别人，也不会和人争执。” 我非常钦佩他。在Y Combinator以及我们的个人生活中他所做的一切都令人敬佩，我从他身上学到了很多。（01:15:53）：从丈夫身上学习是件挺无聊的事，但同时我要再多说几句。我从我们投资的创始人身上学到了很多。他们中有些人非常了不起，历经千辛万苦，成功创立了令人惊叹的公司，远超我们投资时所预料。其中许多人都是非常棒的人，现在他们还经常教导我。比如布莱恩·切斯基。他从学生变成了老师。他对商业经营比我懂得多得多，我经常向他寻求建议。能在创业圈被这么多聪明人包围，我真是幸运极了。毕竟作为一个创业迷，我可以整天谈论创业，思考创业相关的问题，有这么多人围绕着我，支持着我，真是太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Would you believe that a cereal experience led to a 92 billion business today? I just looked it up, how big they've gotten.
turns.zh: 你能相信，一次谷物麦片的创业经历最终成就了如今市值920亿美元的商业帝国吗？我刚刚查了一下，他们的发展实在令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Honestly, I wouldn't. I wish I could say, "Oh, I knew they'd be this big." But the truth is, with all of the super successful startups, yeah you can remember feeling very positively about them and certainly feeling like, as they went along in the first few years, like they're doing really well, they're really determined, they're doing a great job, but you just never really think. They themselves, probably didn't realize that they'd ever be that big. Let's face it. That's just the way startups are.
turns.zh: 说实话，我还真不信。真希望能说一句：“哦，我早料到他们会这么成功。”但现实是，面对那些超级成功的初创公司，你确实会对它们心怀好感——尤其是初创阶段的头几年。看着它们势头正劲、意志坚定、工作出色，但你从未真正预料到它们会发展到如此规模。说实话，这些初创公司创始人自己可能也从未想过能做到今天的规模。面对现实吧，这就是初创公司的特质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Here's the actual final question. Is there a fun story of early days YC, whether it's with Airbnb founders or Paul or anything that comes to mind as just like, wow, what a different time that was, or what a surprising thing that happened then?
turns.zh: 好的。现在来回答最后一个问题。YC早期有没有什么趣事？无论是Airbnb创始人与保罗的故事，还是其他能让人感叹“那真是截然不同的时代”或“当时发生的惊人事件”的故事？

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: It's funny you ask, because actually one of my ideas I've had lately is that I want to start thinking about writing sort of a YC biography kind of book. I don't know when the time is, but the point is, I have to remember things because it's hard. When it's been 20 years to go way back, you have to remember specific things that happened. YC, I just remember the early days being so magical and so pure. When we started, no one knew about us, no one was bothering us. We just did what we were doing with no distractions. We were helping, albeit a very small group of founders, eight in that first summer, we were just doing what we loved doing and growing organically. And no one was scrutinizing us or blaming us for things or writing negative news stories about us. The negative stories in the press, because I'm a people-person and I'm very sensitive, Paul's not as sensitive as me, and so he doesn't care if there's a negative story in the press that's not true. (01:19:09): I do. It really affected me, and I hated when we got big enough that people would lie about us and say bad things. So I look back fondly when we first started of it was the most fun time of my life, the most productive time of my life, didn't have kids then, and I could just help the founders and learn about all these exciting things that happened in the startup world, because it was new to me then, the startup world was new when we started Y Combinator, so I had a lot of learning to do. And I met all these cool people, and it was just very authentic, no one was doing it to be cool.
turns.zh: 你问得真巧，因为最近我确实有个想法——我想开始构思一本关于YC的传记书籍。虽然还不确定具体时间，但关键是，我必须努力回忆往事，因为这太难了。回首20年前的往事，你必须清晰记得那些具体事件。YC早期阶段真是充满魔力与纯粹。刚起步时，没人听说过我们，也没人打扰我们。我们专心致志地做事，全心投入，帮助八位初创者（首个夏天仅有八位）做着自己热爱的事，自然成长。没有人审视我们、指责我们，也没有负面新闻攻击我们。那些负面报道让我很受伤——因为我是个很在意他人看法的人，而保罗没那么敏感，所以他不在乎媒体上的不实报道。但我很在意。我讨厌看到公司规模变大后，人们编造谎言、恶意攻击我们。所以回首初创时期，那是我人生中最开心的时光，也是最富有成效的阶段——那时我还没孩子，可以全心全意帮助初创者们，了解创业界所有激动人心的动态，因为那时创业界对我来说是全新的。我结识了许多优秀的人，那个时代非常纯粹，没有人是为了耍酷而创业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Well, let me ask maybe one other question. Was there a moment when you felt like YC was working? When it felt like, wow, maybe this is going to make it?
turns.zh: 好的。最后再问一个问题：有没有某个时刻让你确信YC模式行之有效？有没有某个瞬间让你觉得：“哇，也许这真的能成功？”

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: There were sort of two moments that I remember I felt like YC was working, because remember, we started Y Combinator as 100% like an experiment. Could we fund younger founders with small amounts of money? That was it. Then that summer we created this batch investment idea, and then that became the idea of funding them in batches. And that was the first aha moment was after that first summer when we invited people to participate in the Summer Founders Program, which is what it was called. And remember, that first summer had Sam Altman, Emmett Shear, Justin Kan, Alexis and Steve of Reddit, they were in the first batch. And the batch thing worked really well because they all became friends. We could have dinner every week, and bring in guest speakers and then introduce them to investors at demo day, and that whole batch-investing thing was an aha moment and we said, "Oh my gosh, let's keep doing this. This really works." And so that was a moment where we knew we were onto something, and that's when we then did it in California in the winter. (01:21:11): But the second big moment was probably, I remember it was like a year later, and no reporter would write about us, investors really didn't think that much of us, but I remember when Reddit got bought by Condé Nast in 2006. It was that, and then at the same time, I think it was like Charles River Ventures or one of these Boston, maybe it wasn't even Boston, but it was a VC firm, did the seed program where they invested maybe a 100K in startups, and the press loved that. They wrote all about this $100,000 investment, and they'd sort of mentioned Y Combinator as doing small investments. And then that, coupled with the Reddit press, sort of made us feel like, oh my gosh, we are sort of legitimate, and the eyes of outsiders became sort of aware of who we were. And I sort of felt like we've arrived, we've been in the press, people are finally paying attention.
turns.zh:
让我印象深刻的有两个时刻，让我觉得YC模式行之有效。记得我们最初创办Y Combinator完全是作为一个实验——我们能否用少量资金资助年轻创业者？仅此而已。那个夏天，我们提出了批量投资的理念，随后形成了分批次资助创业者的模式。第一个突破点出现在第一个夏天，当时我们邀请人们参加名为"夏季创始人计划"的项目。记得那个夏天有山姆·奥特曼、埃米特·希尔、贾斯汀·坎、Reddit的亚历克西斯和史蒂夫，他们都是首批参与者。批量投资模式效果显著，因为他们都成了好朋友。我们每周共进晚餐，邀请嘉宾演讲，在Demo Day将他们介绍给投资者。整个批量投资模式堪称灵光一现，我们感叹："天哪，继续做下去吧，这真的有效！" 从那一刻起，我们意识到自己找到了正确的方向，并在当年冬天将模式引入加州。

（01:21:11）第二个关键时刻大概是一年后，当时没有记者愿意报道我们，投资者对我们也不太重视。但我记得2006年Reddit被康泰纳仕收购后，加上查尔斯河风投或波士顿某家风投公司推出10万美元种子基金项目，媒体大肆报道。这两件事让YC获得了认可，外界开始关注我们。我感觉我们终于站稳脚跟，获得了媒体关注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. And it's funny that Reddit just went public, it's kind of the other side of that coin.
turns.zh: 太了不起了。有趣的是，Reddit刚刚上市了，这正好印证了事情的两面性。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: I know. Pretty impressive. Definitely didn't necessarily think that was going to be happening.
turns.zh: 我知道。确实令人惊叹。当时真没想到会发展成这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you have to run, but I can't help but ask around what you just talked about where you decided to invest in batches. You wrote this really interesting point that none of us had any experience angel investing, and that's where the idea of funding startups and batches came from. We decided to fund a bunch of startups at once during the summer so that we could learn how to invest. And I love that your inexperience in doing it, created this structure. That unique weakness/strength is what led to the way YC operates, and I think that's really interesting.
turns.zh: 我知道你得走了，但我还是忍不住想问问你刚才说的关于分批投资的那些事儿。你提到一个很有意思的观点——我们之前都缺乏天使投资的经验，所以才萌生出资助初创企业和分批投资的想法。今年夏天，我们决定一次性资助多家初创公司，这样既能积累投资经验，又能通过实践不断学习。我特别欣赏你这种因缺乏经验而创造出的独特模式。这种独特的弱点/优势，正是YC运作方式的根源所在，我觉得这真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Yeah, we definitely wanted to learn more about how to be investors, so that's when we decided to do this summer founders program where we could invest in a whole bunch at once, and then the plan was to go to asynchronous investing like normal investors, but we realized that there was something magical about this batch thing. So sometimes, I always say we love domain experts, but sometimes maybe ignorance is sort of bliss and you just discover new things.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们确实想更深入地学习如何做投资，所以才策划了今夏的创始人项目，一次性投资多家公司。原本计划像普通投资者那样进行异步投资，但后来我们发现分批投资这种模式有着不可思议的魔力。有时候我总说我们偏爱领域专家，但有时候无知或许也是种福气——你能因此意外发现新机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jessica, this was everything I hoped it would be. We covered so much ground. I think people are going to love it no matter what you think.
turns.zh: 杰西卡，这次对谈完全超出了我的预期。我们探讨了太多深层次的内容。无论你怎么看，我相信听众都会爱上这场对谈的。

turns.speaker: Jessica Livingston
turns.en: Oh, good. Good, good, good.
turns.zh: 哦，太好了。太好了，太好了，太好了。

turns.en: Two final questions. Where can folks check out The Social Radars and anything else you want people to know about? And how can listeners be useful to you?

So I don't do any marketing. So if it resonates with you, if you find an episode interesting, please spread the word and write a review and rating.

turns.en: I was just going to add that, I'm glad you threw that in there. Jessica, thank you so much for being here.

turns.en: Thank you so much, Lenny. It was a lot of fun.
